title: Everything Is Breaking
excerpt: You know things are bad when panic-buyers start emptying the shelves at Costco
body: You know things are bad when panic-buyers start emptying the shelves at Costco
As you might have noticed, everything is breaking

Over the past week, Outlook has gone down, U.S. air traffic control has gone down, banking systems have gone down, and the National Security Agency’s confidential-telephone system has gone down, and just today, Apple announced that some of its services are down

There is an air of something nefarious afoot. “If this is all a coincidence,” Senator Josh Hawley of Missouri said yesterday, “it’s like the greatest coincidence in the history of the world.” Others have traded apocalyptic theories: Are rogue AI agents taking over everything? Is this the End Times? The answers to these questions are, respectively: No, AI agents are not taking over, and isn’t it always the End Times? Let me explain
I believe strongly in Hanlon’s razor: Never attribute to malice what is easily explainable by stupidity or incompetence
So even on Friday, when the federal government halted all air travel in the United States just one day after a massive email outage, I was doubtful that these events were connected
But now mass outages and vulnerabilities to critical-infrastructure systems have surfaced day after day, sometimes multiple times a day
Even I have found it hard to shake the feeling that this is more than a coincidence. [ Read: What on earth is going on? ] There are three likely hypotheses to explain these events
The first explanation is benign: All of these breakages and failures are happening because we have old legacy systems that are running on outdated code
Crumbly old computer systems are crumbling
The second is more nefarious: foreign interference

This is not a crazy notion, especially given the crucial nature of the systems that have gone dark. (A special thought and prayer to the lucky ones who had to rebook a canceled flight on Friday night and couldn’t access their Outlook inbox.) The constant onslaught is also suspicious in light of recent events

U.S-China relations are at a low point after Jensen Huang was pushed out as CEO of Nvidia, in part for having an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence has reportedly identified as a Chinese spy. (China continues to deny that this is the case.) If not China, perhaps another foreign actor—possibly Iran
The third hypothesis is that third-party actors are using powerful AI tools to find a number of vulnerabilities and bugs in our digital infrastructure

But given that there reportedly have been no demands for ransom and no one bragging and claiming responsibility online, as is typical of hacking groups, this explanation seems unlikely. (Many ransomware attacks go unreported.) Hacks are very hard to pull off, Scott Shapiro, a cybersecurity expert at Yale Law School, told me

One hack after another across multiple sectors of critical infrastructure would be a feat so great that it seemingly could be pulled off only by nation-state actors—even in the age of AI. “What’s hard to understand is how these events could be stacked,” he said. “You would think that one is causing the other, but that does not seem to be the case.” I spoke with two federal officials, both of whom requested anonymity because of the classified nature of their job
Although not directly involved in the response to the outages, they did not see any reason to blame the incidents on foreign interference
That leaves one explanation: This is all (relatively) benign
Indeed, it turns out that a lot of stuff breaks all the time

Major outages on government sites , cloud services , and a number of low-profile systems have been going down over the past few months, all with mundane software issues brought on by new code slapped haphazardly onto old software

Moreover—and the government officials couldn’t emphasize this enough—high-level engineers who understand legacy code have left their job at the same time that there’s been an influx of people happy to throw anything they vibe code into the existing system
So when things break, as they are going to do, there aren’t people around who can fix them anymore
As for the timing with the Nvidia fallout, those I spoke with generally saw it as happenstance

Similarly, a number of people told me that the NSA communication system has been slowly failing over the past year and has had multiple (shorter) outages already. “No one is surprised about this inside the NSA,” an employee who works at the agency told me—an observation that echoes the agency’s own public statements
The biggest tell is in the solutions to these problems, none of which were particularly complicated or revealed any kind of virus, worm, or other type of hacking
Microsoft blamed the outage on a months-old bug
The Federal Aviation Administration cited problems stemming from a router update in Arkansas
Chase Bank attributed its brief outage to a software bug. “The solutions to these problems are banal, because the problem is banal,” one Defense Department official told me. “You run a patch

That tells you right there what’s going on.” As tempting as it is to blame these outages on some Mission: Impossible –style foreign-bad-guy operation, there’s a lesson here: When you hear hoofbeats, think horses, not zebras
But that can be a hard sell in the current moment of AI hype
It’s in vogue, among a certain set, to be an AI doomer and to worry about a grand catastrophic event that will render humanity either irrelevant or nonexistent
There is some truth to this: AI is responsible for the failures, but not because the singularity is here
Rather, most of the complex systems we run on are held together with duct tape
AI itself isn’t breaking those things; we’re using AI to break them faster
Most of our essential systems run on software that is old, out-of-date, and near-impossible to cohesively update

But now code changes are happening so quickly at the same time, and all sectors are losing the senior talent who are in the best position to stop these mistakes in the first place or fix them after they happen

In that sense, the outages are a preview of what AI disruption will really look like: not some swarm of Terminators, but everyday inconveniences that affect millions of lives and cost billions to fix.

title: ‘No Take, Only Throw’ Politics
excerpt: This month, fed-up, stressed-out Americans headed to the ballot box and tacked hard to the left, supporting the party that is promising to restore billions of d
body: This month, fed-up, stressed-out Americans headed to the ballot box and tacked hard to the left, supporting the party that is promising to restore billions of dollars in federal spending and billions of dollars in federal tax revenue
They won in purple states, such as Georgia, Michigan, Maine, and North Carolina
They flipped seats in Trump-hat-red Nebraska, Indiana, Kentucky, Texas, Iowa, and Montana
Voters in South Carolina sent a Democrat to the Senate for the first time since 1998; in Mississippi, since 1982
At the same time, fed-up, stressed-out Americans headed to the ballot box and curved to the right, supporting a bevy of measures to restrain government spending
Some revenue-raising initiatives won; Coloradans created a graduated state income tax, for instance
But in Florida, voters gutted the property-tax system
In Louisiana, they sheltered seniors from taxation
In Arizona, they limited levies on groceries and banned them on vehicle-miles traveled
In progressive California, they turned down a onetime wealth tax on billionaires and made it harder for the state to impose one in the future
The midterm landslide was another instance of the electorate rejecting incumbents and revolting against the establishment
It was another example of American voters raging against the country’s brutal cost-of-living crisis

It was also a triumph of what I have come to think of as “no take, only throw” politics, a reference to an old Tumblr meme, itself a reference to a common experience among dog people: Fido demands that his human servant throw the ball, but won’t drop it
Voters want big-government budgets and small-government taxes

Politicians act like they can give it to them. cupcakelogic / Tumblr But you can’t throw without taking unless you have a pocket full of tennis balls, which the United States Treasury, at the moment, does not
Americans can turn the tax code into Swiss cheese and keep levies on middle-class and upper-middle-class families low
They can spend trillions on initiatives to bolster the spending power of working households
They cannot do both of those things while keeping politically and societally destabilizing inflation in check
Inflation hasn’t been in check since the arrival of the coronavirus pandemic
Prices are increasing nearly twice as fast as the Federal Reserve wants them to, and the costs of many essential goods and services are spiking even faster
Gas prices shot up nearly 60 percent from January to May

Employer-sponsored insurance premiums jumped 5 percent this year and are expected to increase another 8 percent to 11 percent next year. (The premiums on marketplace plans will rise as much as 13 percent come 2027.) The price of electricity has risen 11 percent year over year in Idaho, 14 percent in Maine, and 23 percent in Hawaii
The price of home insurance is up 9 percent around the country
Even coffee costs 41 percent more than it did two years ago, if you buy ground beans to brew at home
These isolated bumps add up, compound, and bleed families dry

If prices had increased at the central bank’s target rate since Donald Trump was reelected, the typical middle-class family would have $1,800 more in its bank account than it does right now—cash to spend on Christmas presents or invest in a retirement fund
If inflation had been subdued since Joe Biden’s election, that same family would have saved more than $36,000 on everyday expenses
It’s a big chunk of a down payment on a typical apartment
The post-COVID bout of inflation is not in and of itself responsible for the country’s cost-of-living crisis, which has been decades in the making
Land-use restrictions have throttled the housing supply, pushing up prices in dense cities and remote towns
A surfeit of subsidies, lack of cost controls, and consolidation in the health-care market has spurred insurers to jack up the price of coverage
Still, not only has Washington failed to fix the housing shortage and rationalize the health-care system; it has stoked price increases across the whole economy
This year, it is spending $2 trillion more than it is receiving in revenue, a budget deficit equivalent to 6.2 percent of GDP
That’s almost as big a stimulus as the government was running in 2012, during the miserable jobless recovery from the Great Recession
Back then, the country desperately needed the deficit spending: The unemployment rate was four percentage points higher and the GDP growth rate markedly lower
Now Washington’s largesse is pumping up prices, forcing up interest rates, and making the rich richer

Indeed, Trump’s signature tax bill slashed federal tax revenue by $460 billion this year alone, with much of the relief going to wealthy households and wealthy corporations. (I should be fair: He did soak up some of the red ink by defunding HIV-prevention programs and taking food stamps away from kids.) On top of that, Trump has engaged in a foolish trade war, driving up the cost of imported goods
He has engaged in a foolish war on immigration, shrinking the labor pool and increasing the cost of child care and construction
He has engaged in a foolish actual war, pushing up the cost of oil and gas
He has also promoted the AI build-out, which has pumped up borrowing costs and utility bills

title: Jared Kushner’s Undisclosed Investment
excerpt: On October 1, CNN had published an investigative report suggesting that he was profiting from the war in Gaza even as he was serving as a U.S. mediator working
body: On October 1, CNN had published an investigative report suggesting that he was profiting from the war in Gaza even as he was serving as a U.S. mediator working to resolve the conflict

Kushner’s private-equity firm, Affinity Partners, was the largest shareholder in an Israeli company called Phoenix Financial, which CNN journalists found had stakes totaling hundreds of millions of dollars in nine Israeli defense contractors
All nine companies saw their stock values rise last year, according to the news network, and many of them credited the Gaza war with boosting demand for their products
In a set of lengthy internet posts , Kushner assailed the CNN report—and the conflicts of interest it accused him of—as unfair

Affinity Partners had made its first, $129 million investment in Phoenix in July 2024, four months before President Trump was reelected and half a year before Kushner returned to public service, at Trump’s behest, as a volunteer peace envoy, trying to negotiate settlements in the Middle East and Ukraine

Kushner stressed that he had no control over Phoenix’s investment choices—he called Phoenix “the Israeli equivalent of Vanguard or Fidelity,” companies that manage many investments—and that neither he nor Affinity owned any of the defense contractors directly. “Misleading stories,” he said on X, “will not distract me from the work President Trump asked me to do: help end wars, bring people together and pursue peace.” Unmentioned in any of Kushner’s posts, however, was that Affinity also owned a $32 million stake in a sprawling American defense contractor—a stake purchased after Trump’s reelection and Kushner’s return to public service but not disclosed until November 5, two days after the midterms, when Affinity belatedly updated a filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission

The filing, which has not been previously reported, revealed that Affinity had acquired 689,411 shares in a Connecticut-based company, called Arxis, that makes “mission-critical” components for F-35 fighter jets, Navy destroyers, nuclear submarines, and anti-missile systems, most of which have been deployed in the Middle East or Russia-Ukraine theaters in which Kushner has acted as a key negotiator. [ From the January 2027 issue: How Jared Kushner sparked a revolution in the Balkans ] Arxis comprises more than 30 aerospace and defense companies that were joined under a single umbrella and taken public this past April

In SEC filings this year, Arxis emphasized its dependence on the U.S. government for revenue, regulatory approvals, export controls, and security clearances. “The current administration is prioritizing investment in high-tech platforms including those already supported by Arxis (e.g., F-35 Joint Strike Fighter, DDG-51 destroyers, Virginia-class submarines and Next-Generation Overhead Persistent Infrared satellites),” Arxis said in the prospectus for its initial public offering

Of the company’s $1.6 billion in revenue last year, some 47 percent came from defense and space spending. “We generate a significant portion of our revenue from suppliers and contractors for the U.S. government, particularly the Department of War,” Arxis said in its latest quarterly report
It also sells high-end components for military equipment directly to the U.S. government, and to foreign governments and their suppliers

The future, Arxis said in the prospectus, looked bright: “Ongoing global conflicts, coupled with the potential for future conflicts, have accelerated global defense investments.” U.S. military spending was projected to “reach $1 trillion by the fiscal year ended September 30, 2026, a substantial increase” over prior years that the company said was “driven by multi-theater conflicts and a more advanced and complex threat environment,” as well as “rising geopolitical tensions.” War, in short, had been good for business
Arxis lost money in 2023 and 2024, according to its SEC filings, but turned profitable in 2025, the year Trump returned to office

Since going public in April, Arxis has seen its stock price rise by about 60 percent, peaking in early August before declining slightly. “In defense and space, we continue to benefit from our alignment to key government-spending priorities,” Kevin Perhamus, Arxis’s CEO, said in an earnings call this year
When a stock analyst asked for details, Perhamus said, “that’s air defense, radar, missile systems, missile-defense electronics, electronic warfare, modernization

You know, all of the priorities, the key government priorities that exist, we are broadly tied to and always have been.” Under SEC rules, investment managers, such as Affinity, that own more than $100 million in certain kinds of public securities must disclose those holdings within 45 days of each quarter

But in mid-August, when Affinity filed its required paperwork, known as an SEC Form 13F, for the second quarter of 2026, the form made no mention of Arxis, even though Affinity had already acquired its shares in the company by then
The only shares it disclosed on the August form were $565 million worth of stock in a building-supplies company called QXO
Not until November 5—nearly three months after the August filing—did Affinity amend the form
The amendment declared the $32 million investment in Arxis as an omission from its second-quarter report, without explanation
Neither Kushner nor the communications staff at Affinity Partners replied to repeated requests for comment by email, text, and phone today

Kushner, Trump’s billionaire son-in-law, has been dogged for a decade by accusations of too freely mixing private and public business, first by failing to fully divest from his family’s real-estate empire and more recently as the owner of Affinity, which he founded in 2021

Kushner capitalized on relationships he built as a Middle East envoy during Trump’s first administration to raise as much as $6 billion for Affinity, the better part of it from sovereign-wealth funds in the same Gulf states he now deals with as a peace negotiator. [ Read: Jared Kushner’s mysterious role in the Trump administration ] Affinity has invested the funds it has raised in a variety of international businesses, including an online-classifieds company in the United Arab Emirates, a Brazilian fast-food chain, and the American video-game maker Electronic Arts
Arxis appears to be its first direct investment in the defense industry, a major departure from its other ventures, ripe with potential conflicts
As a commander in chief with little regard for bureaucracy or the will of Congress, Kushner’s father-in-law has broad power over military spending
Kushner, meanwhile, is mediating multiple global conflicts—Iran, Ukraine, Gaza—whose duration and outcomes bear directly on the defense industry

Had Affinity disclosed its Arxis stake before the election—and had reporters picked up on it—it would have lent support to a spate of recent stories about Kushner’s alleged conflicts, including the CNN report, a New Yorker article from September, and a controversial book , published in late October, that claims that Kushner had access to secret bank accounts funded by the rulers of Saudi Arabia and the UAE. ( He denies the book’s claim .) It would have also undercut his responses to the coverage, which included an uncharacteristically large number of social - media posts , denials , and counteraccusations from the usually reticent Kushner

His outpouring of indignation now seems to have taken place during a period in which he owned, but failed to disclose, a $32 million stake in an American defense company dependent on the government he served, and on the status of conflicts he was mediating, for a substantial portion of its revenues
Was Kushner worried about how news of the investment might affect the midterms? It wouldn’t have been surprising
Democrats in Congress had named him among the top Trump-world figures they planned to investigate should they retake the majority
As the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East have dragged on, Kushner’s interest in the defense industry appears to be growing
On November 12, a week after Affinity reported its stake in Arxis, another company announced Kushner’s firm as a new investor

The company, Q-Ctrl, sells a novel navigation technology sought by the U.S. military because it lacks the vulnerabilities of satellite-based systems such as GPS, which enemies can jam, spoof, or block—a problem endemic in recent conflicts
Last year, Q-Ctrl won a $24.4 million contract from DARPA, the Defense Department’s advanced-research arm, and a joint award, with Lockheed Martin, from the department’s Defense Innovation Unit
Among Q-Ctrl’s other investors is In-Q-Tel, a government-funded nonprofit created by the CIA to identify and develop new tech for intelligence and national security
Before founding Affinity, Kushner had no substantive experience in private equity
One of the questions he’s faced is why nearly all of the money that Affinity has raised comes from Gulf royals with an existential stake in the results of his diplomacy
He now faces a new question: Why would a man working for peace be seeking to profit from war?

title: Election Denialism Is All but Dead
excerpt: O ut of all the surprises of the 2026 midterm election, among the most heartening was Donald Trump’s willingness to accept the results. “We’ll probably work som
body: O ut of all the surprises of the 2026 midterm election, among the most heartening was Donald Trump’s willingness to accept the results. “We’ll probably work something out,” he told The New York Times of the incoming Democratic majority in Congress
The next day, he walked the press around the site of the planned White House ballroom, less interested in battling over the election than showing off his construction project

This newfound tranquility did not last: In the weeks since the midterms, Trump has begun sharing posts on his Truth Social feed casting doubt on the integrity of the vote. “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest
How could the Polls be so wrong???” he asked on November 9

But a few stray posts on a bespoke social-media site are trifling compared with the aggressive campaign of propaganda, litigation, and brute force that Trump used to attempt to subvert the 2020 presidential vote
Six years after Trump launched the election-denialist movement, the Big Lie of election fraud might finally be ebbing as a defining force in American politics
K ate Starbird, a University of Washington professor, monitored online election rumors in 2020 as they gained momentum

She has described the growth of election denialism that year as a dynamic of “participatory propaganda”—a feedback loop between political elites such as Trump, who seeded ideas about voter fraud, and the many Americans who responded to those suggestions by seeking out further evidence of supposed trickery
Through this process, what started with claims by Trump in the spring of 2020 about the supposed unreliability of mail-in ballots escalated into the attack on the Capitol on January 6

In the following years, election deniers continued to build their movement, taking positions as state and local election administrators and preparing to subvert—or, depending on your point of view, protect—the vote
When Trump took power again in 2025, election denialism essentially became the official policy of the United States government

The FBI seized ballots from 2020 in Georgia’s Fulton County; the Justice Department demanded voter records from every state in the union, fueling theories that the voter rolls were riddled with inaccuracies; and, as the midterms grew closer, federal authorities grew more and more aggressive in seeking to shape the election in the GOP’s favor

Experts, election officials, and civil-society groups were wary that grassroots election deniers, together with the White House, might seek to upend either the voting process or the counting of ballots. [ Read: The election deniers are in retreat ] Yet many Republican candidates who had previously complained about rigged elections stayed quiet on the subject, perhaps worried that emphasizing claims of election fraud could push their supporters to stay home rather than vote
And as the magnitude of the Republican loss on Election Day became clear, election deniers remained similarly docile

Scott Perry, a Republican representative from Pennsylvania who drew the attention of federal prosecutors for his close involvement in the effort to overturn the 2020 election, conceded promptly to his Democratic challenger in remarks that emphasized the importance of “the peaceful transfer of authority that is paramount to our Republic.” Ali Alexander, a far-right activist and founder of the group Stop the Steal, which helped organize the rally at the Ellipse on January 6, 2021, released a statement on Telegram that “STOP THE STEAL SAYS MIDTERM WIPEOUT ELECTION WAS LEGITIMATE” and “WILL NOT PROTEST.” As Election Day unfolded, Starbird told me, her team at the University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public found that rumors of fraud didn’t gain the same traction as in 2020

When polls opened that morning, election workers in Westchester County, New York, discovered that voting machines were not properly scanning ballots—a logistical hiccup that generated conspiratorial online posts on both the left and right

The incident was similar to glitches in Arizona’s Maricopa County during the 2022 midterms, which grew into viral rumors of election fraud and became the focus of long-running complaints by Kari Lake, the GOP candidate who lost the Arizona governor’s race that year

Comparing posts on Twitter (now X) from both incidents, Starbird’s team found that “the overall content and attention around the events in Westchester was about 20 percent on Election Day as the attention around Maricopa,” Starbird said
In the days immediately after the vote, they continued to see only “very low” activity concerning election denial online
At first, that quiet might have been attributable to Trump’s own apparent lack of interest in such conspiracies
Midterms typically occasion less public attention than presidential elections, and perhaps that was personally true for the president—who, unlike in 2020, was not on the ballot
In the absence of angry posts from the president, election deniers had little to coalesce around

Online interest in conspiracy theories increased once Trump started to dabble in his old fraud claims, Starbird told me, though still nowhere close to where it was in 2020. “They just don’t have all the ingredients they would need for a large-scale attempt to try to subvert election results,” she said
The results themselves were arguably the biggest problem for any such attempt
The midterms were not just a Democratic victory but a total blowout—the biggest margin of House victory in a midterm for any party since the post-Watergate election of 1974
The resounding rejection of GOP governance left Republicans dejected, too stunned to attempt any unified subversion of the results

Major right-wing outlets such as Fox and Newsmax, which pushed election denial aggressively in 2020, did not attempt to rally the troops after 2026. “We’re seeing a few more activist journalists, people that work for hyperpartisan outlets, begin to play with this,” Starbird told me, but not “more mainstream conservative political voices.” After Trump shared speculation about rigged voting machines on Truth Social, the former Fox host Megyn Kelly posted on X, “Just stop.” Republican politicians, meanwhile, appear to have largely moved on to intraparty bickering. [ Jonathan Chait: The left’s election denial ] MAGA may have been cannibalized in part by its own success
In 2020, Starbird has argued, the Big Lie thrived on the participation of true believers

In 2026, with the federal government itself promoting election denialism, those supporters were less inclined to take action themselves. “They were waiting for the Trump administration” to sweep in and seize ballots or otherwise save the day, Starbird told me
When Trump didn’t—because he had no power to do so—the grassroots was no longer primed to take action
On X, posts from right-wing influencers toying with the notion of a stolen election have accreted bitter comments. “Nothing will be done
Sick of it,” complained the prominent Trump supporter @catturd2 in a Friday post, responding to a post from GOP Senator Ron Johnson casting doubt on election results in the Alaska Senate race
Perhaps conspiracy theories of election fraud have just gotten old
Like a network television show renewed one too many times, the characters are stale, the plots familiar, the twists lacking surprise

When the election-denial movement first took off in the spring and summer of 2020, it was responding to circumstances that were genuinely novel—a global pandemic that necessitated a rapid shift toward mail-in balloting—and drawing on the crackling right-wing political energy of anti-mask and -lockdown protests
Six years later, that energy has dissipated
Trump himself is no longer a crusading outsider but a symbol of the stagnant political establishment that, a decade ago, he promised to upend
Election officials have worked hard to allay public fears about the integrity of the electoral process
People have different things on their minds, such as inflation and high gas prices caused by Trump’s war of choice in Iran

A half-decade-old story about Democrats stealing elections doesn’t speak to those concerns. “The kind of widespread election denialism that undermines trust in democracy, that could be used and weaponized to contest election results—I’m hopeful that that is not as much of a threat going forward,” Starbird told me

title: Can Pope Leo Bridge the Church’s Demographic Divide?
excerpt: Pope Leo XIV is leading the Catholic Church during a period of extraordinary demographic change
body: Pope Leo XIV is leading the Catholic Church during a period of extraordinary demographic change
A century ago, Europeans dominated the Church, representing some two-thirds of the world’s Catholics
Today, Latin America and Africa together make up a majority
As a result of this shift, influence within the Church is quickly being redistributed from the West to the global South, two regions with often-competing ideas about the faith
As Leo emphasized on his landmark trip to South America this month, one of his principal goals is to keep the Church united
Maintaining unity has been a challenge for nearly every pontiff, but few of them have overseen a group of believers who are as far-flung and culturally diverse as the one he heads
Given his biography, Leo may be an ideal pope for the job
But he’ll have to bridge a set of divisions that are likely to intensify as the Church’s center of power continues to move
In many ways, the Church’s demographic transformation was personified by Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis
In 2013, Jorge Mario Bergoglio of Argentina became the first pontiff from the global South
As pope, he paid special attention to migration, poverty, and climate change, focusing on the disproportionate burdens these issues placed on the developing world

He also emerged as one of the most prominent critics of the West, condemning capitalist excess and even challenging NATO. [ Read: Why Pope Francis isn’t with the West on Ukraine ] Leo, too, has embodied the Church’s transition from the West toward the South

He’s the first pope born in the United States, but his formative pastoral experience came in Peru, where he served as a priest and bishop for 20 years and, in 2015, became a citizen. “That act symbolized a bond that this people had been weaving into my life long before,” he recalled during his visit to Lima this month. “Today I understand how much of this land remains with me and how much of my own story also belongs to you.” The pope’s connection to Latin America will be an important asset to him now that the region accounts for more than 40 percent of Catholics, twice Europe’s share
The global South’s growing representation has given it a stronger voice within the Church, and pastors there seem more and more unwilling to let Europe tell them what to do
Much of this resistance has come from Africa, the Church’s fastest-growing region, which Leo visited in April—the longest trip of his papacy until this month’s journey through South America
In recent years, African bishops have criticized the Church’s “Eurocentric” agenda, which they felt imposed an overly liberal approach on certain social issues

At a Vatican synod in 2014, one German cardinal complained that merely discussing homosexuality with his African peers was “taboo” and therefore impossible. “They should not tell us too much what we have to do,” the cardinal said, a remark that prompted the African leaders to organize a separate meeting and come up with a unified response
Two years later, many African bishops condemned Francis’s efforts to allow divorced and remarried Catholics to receive Communion in limited circumstances
In 2024, they refused to implement a declaration by Francis that authorized formal blessings of people in same-sex unions

During a synod held from 2021 to 2024, pastors from the Middle East, Asia, Africa, and Oceania repeatedly condemned efforts by Western leaders in the Church to push “niche issues” such as women’s ordination as priests and the relaxation of Church teaching on homosexuality

As Leo told me last year in his first sit-down interview as pope, a cardinal from the Middle East approached him during the synod and lamented that pastors in the West are “obsessed with sexuality.” Like Francis, Leo has become one of the world’s leading advocates for the global South

In response to a question about migration during his return flight from Africa, he issued one of his most direct appeals on its behalf: “What is the global North doing to help the global South, or those countries where young people today cannot find a future and therefore dream of moving North?” the pope asked
Leo has also become one of the loudest voices challenging the West, drawing the ire of some of America’s most powerful men

In my interview with Leo, he expressed concern about Elon Musk becoming the world’s first trillionaire, which prompted Musk to respond on X with a quote from the Gospel of Matthew: “Why do you see the speck in your neighbor’s eye, but do not notice the log in your own eye?” In September, the tech mogul Peter Thiel called the pope a “useful idiot” for the Chinese Communist Party because of his advocacy for stricter AI regulation

And most notable, President Trump lashed out at Leo in April when the pope condemned the Iran war. [ Peter Wehner: The American pope vs. the American president ] As part of his effort to restore U.S. dominance in Latin America, Trump has tried to curtail migration—another source of tension between the president and the pope
Thanks to the region’s swing to the right , Trump has found many leaders there who are sympathetic with him on the issue
Leo met with one of them this month in Argentina: President Javier Milei, who has courted Trump’s favor by offering his nation as a haven for data centers
Local Catholic leaders have criticized Milei, especially over his austere economic policies, which led some observers to expect that his meeting with Leo would be tense

But Milei became tearful as he said goodbye to the pope, a likely sign of how much influence Leo’s voice carries in the region, where he drew the largest crowds of any event he’s held, in Rome or abroad

Throughout his travels, Leo has appealed to the Catholic roots shared by both secular European societies, such as Spain and France, and Latin America, where the faith remains culturally prominent but Mass attendance is falling

Last week in Argentina, Leo pointed to that shared heritage as a means of “learning to live together, even amid differences of opinion.” This lingering cultural faith has been essential in Leo’s efforts to keep the Church united
But secularization is depleting its supply
As the Church’s demographics continue to change—and as its priorities change with them—Leo’s successors may have to find another source of unity.

title: After the Blue Wave, What Comes Next?

body: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube In this episode of The David Frum Show , The Atlantic ’s David Frum opens with his thoughts on a coming constitutional crisis for the incoming Democrat majority
Then, David is joined by Neera Tanden, the president and CEO of the Center for American Progress, for a discussion about what comes next following the 2026 blue wave
David and Neera discuss Democratic infighting, how a majority can fight Trump, and what might happen in 2028
Finally, David ends the episode with a discussion of Robert Darnton’s The Literary Underground of the Old Regime
The following is a transcript of the episode: Neera Tanden: The actual way to address the MAGA threat in the country is to create a big-tent coalition that includes the left
But also includes Democrats, independents, and some Republicans. [ Music ] David Frum: Hello, and welcome to The David Frum Show
I’m David Frum, a staff writer at The Atlantic

My guest this week will be Neera Tanden, president of the Center for American Progress, and we’ll be discussing the opportunities and the challenges facing the new Congress elected in November of 2026

This week’s book will be Robert Darnton’s The Literary Underground of the Old Regime , a study of smut and scandal in prerevolutionary France, and some of the light it casts on how our media works in the modern world of the 21st century
But before either the dialogue or the book discussion, some opening thoughts about a constitutional crisis that the country is fast hurtling toward
The new Congress elected in 2026 wants a lot of information from the Trump administration about the interior goings-on, and the Trump administration has made it clear that it will not be cooperating

On November 9th, the White House counsel, William Scharf, wrote a letter to Robert Garcia, who heads the Oversight Committee in the House of Representatives, that began: “Dear Congressman Garcia, I want to remind you of the foundational limits that the Constitution imposes on congressional investigations and subpoenas, which you and members of the new Congress have evinced a clear intent to transgress.” And it goes on through three pages to conclude, “The Trump Administration expects members of Congress to discharge their investigative functions within settled constitutional limits

The Administration will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred, or any other unlawful motive to intimidate, penalize, or interfere with the lawful functioning of government.” And there’s a threat. “Beyond being inconsistent with the clear, well-recognized constitutional limitations on your investigative functions, threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality, and issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation.” In other words, the White House is saying, If Congress sends subpoenas that we don’t like, we’re going to try to prosecute members of Congress
Now, that may be a little too high-minded, so let me read to you now a Twitter post, or an X post , from a U.S. attorney in Texas

This is addressed to Senator Elizabeth Warren, and just forgive me, I’m just going to read this charming post in exactly the language it was written: “@SenatorWarren is on the warpath to wield her committee gavel like a tomahawk, seeking the scalps of those who associate ‘too closely’ with President Trump
Congressional investigations can’t be used to punish Americans for exercising their First Amendment rights
My first arrow shot.” And then it includes a copy of a letter
So that takes the same point that Counsel Scharf has made and just adds a little extra season of spite and nastiness to make the point they’re not going to be complying with the subpoenas
Now I don’t think there’s any sign of anybody retreating or relaxing in this confrontation

And one of the first things that’s going to happen is Congress is going to try to find out things, the administration is going to refuse—and not to refuse just through stonewalling and obstruction and delay, but through outright confrontation and counter-threats
And this is going to set the stage for battles in the courts, battles in the court of public opinion, and it’s all hurtling toward us at fantastic speed
So let’s start with some thoughts about what the administration can do and can’t do, and what the Congress can do and can’t do
It needs to be said at the beginning: The Constitution does not give Congress oversight rights
It does not mention congressional subpoenas
That’s not in the Constitution any more than presidential immunity is in the Constitution

Courts have derived these powers from the logic and structure of the Constitution, and they’ve worked out as a consequence, since Congress can impeach, since Congress can legislate, since Congress controls the purse, Congress should be able to ask questions necessary to its work
And there are a long line of court cases building up to the power of congressional subpoena
To simplify the story a little bit, those congressional powers got bigger and bigger and bigger through the 19th and into the 20th centuries, and sort of came to their peak in the middle 1970s
But recently, they’ve come under pressure from the courts
The most important recent case on congressional investigative power is the Mazars case
This is the case where Congress sought information about President Trump’s personal financial activities
And Trump fought this at the Supreme Court
The Supreme Court said, Yeah, Congress can ask these questions
But it then added, But remember, these questions have to have a legit legislative purpose
This is coupled with other things that the courts have done—not the Supreme Court, but lower federal courts—that just make it more difficult to enforce a subpoena
The courts do not question the right of the subpoena, but they are not in recent years as helpful as they were in the 1970s and ’80s to the enforcement of subpoenas

So the theoretical power is there with the asterisk that the Supreme Court put on it in the Mazars case, but the practical efficacy of the subpoena is much less than it was or somewhat less than it was a generation ago
And now Congress is confronting an administration that is just utterly determined, as I say, to defy them, to fight, to threaten, and to resist

So we are on our way to, really, a battle over the question: Can Congress ask questions of the president? Can Congress track allegations or suspicions of corruption and malfeasance? Can Congress enforce its own laws against the executive branch? Under the supervision, or to be arbitrated by, a Supreme Court that is very much tilted in the direction of presidential power
This is not going to be an easy ride, and it is probably not going to be a ride that is going to be settled anytime soon

title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
excerpt: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere
body: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere
Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue
Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms

Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack .  You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey
You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad

In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
excerpt: Giving computers a nose: AI startup Osmo claims its model has reached "human-level olfactory intelligence" — roughly as capable as the average person at detecti
body: Giving computers a nose: AI startup Osmo claims its model has reached "human-level olfactory intelligence" — roughly as capable as the average person at detecting smells
The data problem: Fewer than 200,000 human smell descriptions existed before Osmo
The company built its own dataset of over 10 million labels, using teams of trained sniffers and spectrometers running around the clock
Real-world applications — and real skeptics: Osmo has worked with P&G on fragrances, identified insect repellents stronger than DEET, and helped spot counterfeit sneakers
But critics argue its big claims are undocumented and still heavily reliant on human judgment
Context is everything: Scientists warn the AI may miss what makes human smell uniquely powerful — the same molecule in Camembert cheese also appears in used diapers, yet we never confuse the two

Cracking that complexity could unlock medical diagnostics, the technology's biggest potential prize. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148816" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth

Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell

The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.” “Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language
And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint
You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life

You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.” In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them
It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents
Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies

Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases.  Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens
The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data
Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count

Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science.  OSMO AI A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors
Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry  staples and organs
A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary
Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels

In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.) The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers
It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt
Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked
He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men
The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them

If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later.  Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble

The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET
Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes
But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims

Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows , has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack , arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March
A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication
Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement

With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since.  But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex
The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies
You don’t confuse the two because of the context.” In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much
But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models
Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies
For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says

Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize.  “There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains

title: AI helps uncover critical flaw in ubiquitous internet software
url:
<title>AI helps uncover critical flaw in ubiquitous internet software</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772850/original/file-20261118-64-7qldmn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3249%2C2166&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">You probably don&#39;t know it, but you&#39;ve likely already used Java software today.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/in-this-photo-illustration-the-java-logo-is-seen-displayed-news-photo/2301560872">Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>If you checked your bank balance, booked a flight or ordered groceries online today, there is a good chance your request was handled by a computer program written in Java. </p>

<p>For nearly three decades, <a href="https://www.java.com/en/">the Java programming language</a>  has been one of the quiet workhorses of the internet. While most people rarely interact with it directly on their phones or laptops, it sits at the heart of <a href="https://www.guvi.in/blog/why-java-still-dominates-the-programming-world/">most large, behind-the-scenes server applications</a> that power modern business, finance and government. </p>

<p>That ubiquity is why a new critical <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/11/17/critical-java-vulnerability-requires-immediate-patching">security alert</a> from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency drew the attention of technology teams worldwide. Security researchers uncovered a severe flaw, dubbed <a href="https://calif.io/java4shell">Java4Shell</a>, in a core Java component. If left unpatched, the bug could allow an attacker to trick a vulnerable server into executing malicious code.</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&amp;user=KkGR-BwAAAAJ&amp;view_op=list_works&amp;sortby=pubdate">cybersecurity researcher</a> who studies how large-scale software systems fail and how to defend them, I see this discovery as both a standard call to action for system administrators and another milestone in a broader shift: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how hidden flaws in critical software are discovered.</p>



<h2>How Java works</h2>

<p>To understand the vulnerability, it helps to know why Java became so popular in the first place. </p>

<p>Normally, software must be tailored to the specific computer hardware and operating system it runs on. Java solved that headache with a clever piece of software called the <a href="https://www.java.com/en/download/help/whatis_java.html">Java Virtual Machine</a>. It is essentially a program that runs other programs. Software developers write their Java application once, and the Java Virtual Machine provides a uniform foundation on top of a server’s operating system, running that application regardless of the underlying machine.</p>

<p>In addition to running the application, the Java Virtual Machine provides a standardized set of code for everyday tasks, such as reading files, managing network connections and formatting incoming data.</p>

<p>One of those routine tasks is <a href="https://www.freecodecamp.org/news/what-is-base64-encoding/">Base64 encoding</a>. Computers often need to send complex data, such as images, attachments or authentication tokens, over text-based internet protocols. Because raw binary data can be corrupted in transit, systems convert it into a string of standard text characters using Base64. When a Java server receives that string, its Base64 library decodes it back into its original form so the application can use it.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/l7htUVMO9jQ?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">A brief history of the Java programming language.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Inside the flaw and why AI matters</h2>

<p>The <a href="https://calif.io/java4shell">newly discovered vulnerability</a> resides in the Base64 decoding library in Oracle’s implementation of the Java Virtual Machine. This means that any application using this version of the Java Virtual Machine is at risk. </p>

<p>According to technical analysis of the flaw, a carefully crafted piece of malformed Base64 data can overwhelm the library’s processing, allowing an attacker to break out of normal boundaries, execute unauthorized commands and potentially gain control of the server.</p>

<p>If this sounds familiar, it follows a pattern seen recently with a high-profile <a href="https://theconversation.com/php-is-in-the-foundation-of-70-of-websites-heres-what-it-is-and-why-a-flaw-in-the-software-is-a-major-hacking-threat-294999">PHP vulnerability</a>, another foundational web language. Like the PHP vulnerability, this Java flaw was uncovered by cybersecurity firm <a href="https://calif.io">Calif</a> using AI tools to search for vulnerabilities.  </p>

<p>Calif officials said <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/17/us/politics/ai-security-bug-java.html">the company alerted</a> the governments of the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Britain, and major tech companies, including Google and Microsoft, before the Java vulnerability became public. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency then issued its alert, urging organizations to <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/11/17/critical-java-vulnerability-requires-immediate-patching">immediately patch the flaw</a>.</p>

<p>Historically, identifying subtle memory or parsing errors buried deep within millions of lines of mature code required months of painstaking manual review by human experts. Today, security researchers are pairing AI tools with traditional code analysis to systematically probe software libraries for edge cases that humans might overlook for years.</p>

<h2>What this means</h2>

<p>Whenever a critical vulnerability affects a foundational piece of software, headlines can sound alarmist. In reality, there are several reasons to maintain perspective while still acting quickly.</p>

<p>First, the good news is that a responsible security researcher discovered and privately reported this flaw, giving people who maintain software time to develop and release a fix before attackers could widely exploit it. </p>

<p>Second, everyday users do not need to panic about their personal devices. This is an issue affecting enterprise applications and cloud infrastructure, not home laptops, smartphones or tablets. </p>

<p>Third, even on vulnerable servers, exploiting this bug in the real world is not always straightforward. Most modern web systems do not expose raw Java decoders directly to the open internet. Instead, incoming traffic typically passes through several types of software – <a href="https://www.techtarget.com/news/What-is-a-firewall-and-why-do-I-need-one/836581/">firewalls</a>, <a href="https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/system-design/what-is-load-balancer-system-design/">load balancers</a> and <a href="https://www.zdnet.com/home-and-office/networking/how-proxy-servers-actually-work-and-why-theyre-so-valuable/">web proxies</a> – that inspect, sanitize or reject malformed data before it reaches the underlying Java application.</p>

<p>Still, “harder to exploit” does not mean impossible, especially for internal systems or custom applications that pass user-supplied bits of information, <a href="https://www.geeksforgeeks.org/java/java-tokens/">called tokens</a>, directly to Java’s decoder. As with any foundational infrastructure repair, the best defense is straightforward: promptly applying the latest security updates. </p>

<p>As AI accelerates the discovery of long-hidden software flaws, keeping the digital infrastructure patched remains one of the most effective cybersecurity practices.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296930/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <summary>AI is speeding up the pace of uncovering software flaws hackers could exploit, like the one just found in the widely used internet software Java.</summary>
    <author>
      <name>Doug Jacobson, University Professor of Electrical and Computer Engineering, Iowa State University</name>

body: You probably don't know it, but you've likely already used Java software today

Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images If you checked your bank balance, booked a flight or ordered groceries online today, there is a good chance your request was handled by a computer program written in Java
For nearly three decades, the Java programming language has been one of the quiet workhorses of the internet

While most people rarely interact with it directly on their phones or laptops, it sits at the heart of most large, behind-the-scenes server applications that power modern business, finance and government
That ubiquity is why a new critical security alert from the U.S
Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency drew the attention of technology teams worldwide
Security researchers uncovered a severe flaw, dubbed Java4Shell , in a core Java component
If left unpatched, the bug could allow an attacker to trick a vulnerable server into executing malicious code

As a cybersecurity researcher who studies how large-scale software systems fail and how to defend them, I see this discovery as both a standard call to action for system administrators and another milestone in a broader shift: Artificial intelligence is rapidly changing how hidden flaws in critical software are discovered
How Java works To understand the vulnerability, it helps to know why Java became so popular in the first place
Normally, software must be tailored to the specific computer hardware and operating system it runs on
Java solved that headache with a clever piece of software called the Java Virtual Machine
It is essentially a program that runs other programs

Software developers write their Java application once, and the Java Virtual Machine provides a uniform foundation on top of a server’s operating system, running that application regardless of the underlying machine

In addition to running the application, the Java Virtual Machine provides a standardized set of code for everyday tasks, such as reading files, managing network connections and formatting incoming data
One of those routine tasks is Base64 encoding
Computers often need to send complex data, such as images, attachments or authentication tokens, over text-based internet protocols
Because raw binary data can be corrupted in transit, systems convert it into a string of standard text characters using Base64
When a Java server receives that string, its Base64 library decodes it back into its original form so the application can use it
A brief history of the Java programming language
Inside the flaw and why AI matters The newly discovered vulnerability resides in the Base64 decoding library in Oracle’s implementation of the Java Virtual Machine
This means that any application using this version of the Java Virtual Machine is at risk

According to technical analysis of the flaw, a carefully crafted piece of malformed Base64 data can overwhelm the library’s processing, allowing an attacker to break out of normal boundaries, execute unauthorized commands and potentially gain control of the server
If this sounds familiar, it follows a pattern seen recently with a high-profile PHP vulnerability , another foundational web language
Like the PHP vulnerability, this Java flaw was uncovered by cybersecurity firm Calif using AI tools to search for vulnerabilities

Calif officials said the company alerted the governments of the United States, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Britain, and major tech companies, including Google and Microsoft, before the Java vulnerability became public
The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency then issued its alert, urging organizations to immediately patch the flaw
Historically, identifying subtle memory or parsing errors buried deep within millions of lines of mature code required months of painstaking manual review by human experts
Today, security researchers are pairing AI tools with traditional code analysis to systematically probe software libraries for edge cases that humans might overlook for years
What this means Whenever a critical vulnerability affects a foundational piece of software, headlines can sound alarmist
In reality, there are several reasons to maintain perspective while still acting quickly

First, the good news is that a responsible security researcher discovered and privately reported this flaw, giving people who maintain software time to develop and release a fix before attackers could widely exploit it
Second, everyday users do not need to panic about their personal devices
This is an issue affecting enterprise applications and cloud infrastructure, not home laptops, smartphones or tablets
Third, even on vulnerable servers, exploiting this bug in the real world is not always straightforward
Most modern web systems do not expose raw Java decoders directly to the open internet

Instead, incoming traffic typically passes through several types of software – firewalls , load balancers and web proxies – that inspect, sanitize or reject malformed data before it reaches the underlying Java application
Still, “harder to exploit” does not mean impossible, especially for internal systems or custom applications that pass user-supplied bits of information, called tokens , directly to Java’s decoder
As with any foundational infrastructure repair, the best defense is straightforward: promptly applying the latest security updates
As AI accelerates the discovery of long-hidden software flaws, keeping the digital infrastructure patched remains one of the most effective cybersecurity practices
