<title>Florida’s flooding déjà vu is a sign of things to come – so, who is most at risk and how can they prepare?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772862/original/file-20261118-78-u7bx1o.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Heavy rain inundated already saturated yards in Hollywood, Fla., south of Fort Lauderdale, on Nov. 18, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/daniel-supienski-and-his-daughter-dezirae-supienski-use-a-news-photo/2305738308?phrase=florida%20flooding&amp;adppopup=true">Joe Raedle/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Floodwater filled the streets and crept into homes across Florida’s Atlantic coast as an intense storm dumped <a href="https://www.miamiherald.com/news/local/community/broward/article318133943.html">more than a foot of rain in 24 hours</a> starting Nov. 17, 2026. The deluge followed extreme downpours in parts of the region <a href="https://weather.com/2026/11/03/science/weather-explainers/florida-desert-southwest-flooding-recap-el-nino">less than three weeks earlier</a>, and forecasters <a href="https://balancedweather.substack.com/p/serious-impacts-expected-next-several">warned of more rain still to come</a>.</p>

<p>As people in Fort Lauderdale watched the water rise in their already saturated yards, it may have felt like déjà vu.</p>

<p>In April 2023, more than <a href="https://weather.com/news/weather/news/2023-04-13-fort-lauderdale-most-extreme-united-states-24-hour-rainfall-records">25 inches of rain</a> fell in Fort Lauderdale in 24 hours. <a href="https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/monitoring/scec/records/all/maxp">Even hurricanes</a> rarely drop that much rain in one area that fast. Residents could do little to stop the flooding.  </p>

<p>Studies show that as global temperatures rise, <a href="https://theconversation.com/new-flood-maps-show-us-damage-rising-26-in-next-30-years-due-to-climate-change-alone-and-the-inequity-is-stark-175958">more people will be at risk</a> from such destructive flooding – including in areas that rarely faced extreme flooding in the past.</p>

<p>In many of these communities, the people at greatest risk of harm from flash flooding are <a href="https://theconversation.com/new-flood-maps-show-us-damage-rising-26-in-next-30-years-due-to-climate-change-alone-and-the-inequity-is-stark-175958">low-wage workers</a>, <a href="https://theconversation.com/the-aftermath-of-floods-hurricanes-and-other-disasters-can-be-hardest-on-older-rural-americans-heres-how-families-and-neighbors-can-help-247691">older adults</a> and other vulnerable residents who live in low-lying areas and who have few resources to protect their properties and themselves.</p>



<p>I study the impact of extreme weather on vulnerable communities as an <a href="https://csw.osu.edu/people/our-faculty/rao-smitha-phd/">associate professor of social work</a>. To limit the damage, communities need to know who is at risk and how they can be better prepared.</p>

<h2>More extreme downpours in a warming world</h2>

<p>The Florida storms offer a view into the risks ahead <a href="https://climate.nasa.gov/vital-signs/global-temperature/">as temperatures rise</a>. These risks are especially high as the effects of a strong 2026-27 <a href="https://theconversation.com/as-cities-prepare-for-2026s-super-el-nino-some-crucial-blind-spots-cant-be-ignored-290787">El Niño set in</a>. </p>

<p>A warmer atmosphere <a href="https://theconversation.com/climate-change-is-intensifying-the-water-cycle-bringing-more-powerful-storms-and-flooding-heres-what-the-science-shows-187951">can hold more moisture</a>, leading to stronger downpours. The resulting deluges can be devastating. These events are expected to increase in frequency and intensity in many regions as greenhouse gas emissions from human activities <a href="https://nca5.climate.us/">continue to heat up the planet</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/522724/original/file-20230425-24-nw1p88.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Four maps show how risk of extreme precipitation increased in some regions, particularly the Northeast, and projections of increasing rainfall in the East in the coming decades." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/522724/original/file-20230425-24-nw1p88.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/522724/original/file-20230425-24-nw1p88.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=687&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522724/original/file-20230425-24-nw1p88.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=687&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522724/original/file-20230425-24-nw1p88.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=687&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522724/original/file-20230425-24-nw1p88.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=864&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522724/original/file-20230425-24-nw1p88.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=864&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522724/original/file-20230425-24-nw1p88.png?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=864&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Where extreme precipitation events are forecast to increase under a low-emissions scenario and a high one.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://nca2018.globalchange.gov/chapter/2/">National Climate Assessment 2018</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><a href="https://theconversation.com/repeated-storms-are-turning-disaster-recovery-into-a-way-of-life-and-leaving-communities-facing-disaster-fatigue-287147">Recent disasters</a> show how the risk of flash flooding is expanding beyond <a href="https://theconversation.com/not-in-a-fema-flood-zone-your-home-could-still-be-at-risk-and-you-could-suffer-more-than-your-neighbor-293658">areas traditionally considered at risk</a>. </p>

<h2>Knowing who is most at risk</h2>

<p>To plan for extreme weather, it’s crucial for community leaders and residents to know where the risks are highest and who <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijdrr.2022.103072">might not be prepared</a>.</p>

<p>Low-lying areas with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/01944360708977981">poorly planned development</a>, <a href="https://e360.yale.edu/features/its-not-just-climate-are-we-ignoring-other-causes-of-disasters">lack of investment</a> in protective infrastructure and the lingering effects of <a href="https://www.redfin.com/news/redlining-flood-risk/">historic disinvestment and discrimination</a> are often at higher risk. So are low-income communities with tight budgets that <a href="https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12053-019-09820-z">can’t afford protective measures</a> like upgraded levees or stormwater systems and can’t recover from damage quickly.</p>

<p>When older adults <a href="https://www.samhsa.gov/dtac/disaster-planners/older-adults">live in these flood-prone areas</a>, they are at even higher risk. Older adults have a higher likelihood of having health needs or some form of <a href="https://www.cdc.gov/ncbddd/disabilityandhealth/features/kf-adult-prevalence-disabilities.html">disability</a> that could affect their ability to leave quickly during a disaster. They are also more likely to be <a href="https://www.nia.nih.gov/health/loneliness-and-social-isolation-tips-staying-connected">socially isolated</a>, which may mean they don’t hear timely information or have help to evacuate or quick access to resources for recovering.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="An older man carries a small fuzzy dog while walking through floodwater with a woman waring a backpack." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/522786/original/file-20230425-884-s4af2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/522786/original/file-20230425-884-s4af2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522786/original/file-20230425-884-s4af2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522786/original/file-20230425-884-s4af2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522786/original/file-20230425-884-s4af2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522786/original/file-20230425-884-s4af2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522786/original/file-20230425-884-s4af2n.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Residents walk out of a flooded neighborhood in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., with their pet on April 13, 2023.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/robert-rouilard-and-patricia-polin-evacuate-ginger-from-a-news-photo/1482046569">Joe Raedle/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Renters and the impact of housing insecurity</h2>

<p>My colleagues and I have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2023.102638">examined how prepared people are for disasters</a> of any kind across the U.S. – flooding, tornadoes, hurricanes and others – and how housing security played a role. The numbers are sobering.</p>

<p>Overall, we found in a 2023 study that 57% of the population, among 29,070 housing units surveyed nationwide, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.gloenvcha.2023.102638">reported they were not prepared</a> with food, water, emergency funds and transportation in case disaster struck. We found that households facing housing insecurity – those behind on their payments for rent, mortgage or utilities – were less prepared for disasters than others, even when the occupants had similar incomes and education.</p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A woman standing in floodwater in boots looks in the door of a flooded home. A sign reading 'beware of dog' is in the window. Floodwater is up to  her shins." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/522730/original/file-20230425-14-rm5in4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/522730/original/file-20230425-14-rm5in4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=446&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522730/original/file-20230425-14-rm5in4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=446&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522730/original/file-20230425-14-rm5in4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=446&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522730/original/file-20230425-14-rm5in4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=561&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522730/original/file-20230425-14-rm5in4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=561&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/522730/original/file-20230425-14-rm5in4.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=561&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">For residents with low incomes and without flood insurance, cleanup costs from flooding can be overwhelming.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/tammy-green-walks-into-the-home-she-lives-in-with-her-dad-news-photo/1482256291">Joe Raedle/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>People who are struggling to meet day-to-day needs often don’t have the ability and resources to plan for everyday events, let alone for disasters. Our <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S2212420922002916?via%3Dihub">research</a> has shown that households with children, households led by women, and low-income households were less prepared than others for disasters.</p>

<p>Renting adds additional challenges. In the U.S., <a href="https://www.brookings.edu/essay/us-rental-housing-markets/">lower-income families often depend on the rental market</a>. They tend to move more frequently, and since they don’t own the property, they often can’t make upgrades for safety. And landlords might not prioritize those risks that seem rare but carry costs.</p>

<h2>How to help communities stay safe</h2>

<p>The most effective way to address these challenges is through solutions that are tailored to the community.</p>

<p>That can involve <a href="https://www.americanprogress.org/article/how-fema-can-build-rural-resilience-through-disaster-preparedness/">investing in infrastructure</a>, including state-funded priorities such as drainage systems, large-scale flood prevention measures and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1057/s41599-025-05274-0">strengthening the power grid</a>, as well as ensuring that people have access to <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK316535/">safe and affordable housing</a>. Some communities and federal agencies have <a href="https://www.pew.org/en/research-and-analysis/reports/2022/04/property-buyouts-can-be-an-effective-solution-for-flood-prone-communities">bought out properties</a> that frequently flood and changed zoning rules to prevent more people from moving into harm’s way.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772859/original/file-20261118-64-px0ynz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two people stand in calf-deep floodwater in a street looking at a building." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772859/original/file-20261118-64-px0ynz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772859/original/file-20261118-64-px0ynz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772859/original/file-20261118-64-px0ynz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772859/original/file-20261118-64-px0ynz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772859/original/file-20261118-64-px0ynz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772859/original/file-20261118-64-px0ynz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772859/original/file-20261118-64-px0ynz.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">People walked in flooded roads in Riviera Beach, Fla., on Election Day 2026 near a polling place that had to be relocated because of the first round of November’s severe floods.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/two-people-walk-flooded-roads-near-a-polling-place-that-has-news-photo/2302921618?phrase=florida%20flooding&amp;adppopup=true">Saul Martinez/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Raising community awareness about climate change and extreme weather risks is also crucial, especially among <a href="https://www.apha.org/topics-and-issues/climate-health-and-equity/vulnerable-populations">those most at risk</a>, such as older adults and other <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11111-026-00526-w">socially marginalized groups</a>. </p>

<p>If people understand the risks, know how to prepare their homes, know how to <a href="https://www.fema.gov/pdf/areyouready/basic_preparedness.pdf">plan for emergencies</a>, know whom to contact for help, and have stronger systems of care, they’re more likely to be prepared when disasters strike.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/pNMm90nzT4o?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Scientists explain why warming can lead to heavier downpours and flash flooding.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>I believe the most successful <a href="https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2212420919317893?via%3Dihub">efforts are those that bring at-risk communities into planning discussions</a>.</p>

<p>For example, in Columbus, Ohio, the city partnered with the Central Ohio Area Agency on Aging, <a href="https://agefriendly.osu.edu/engagement/areas-of-commitment/warm-weather-and-aging-resilience-model/">Age Friendly Innovation Center</a> and my team to improve <a href="https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/01634372.2026.2649312">disaster preparedness among older residents</a>. We worked with <a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V-PKDqc2lAc&amp;feature=youtu.be">older adults in affordable housing communities</a> and the human service professionals who support them to help design action plans for communities with special needs in the event of an emergency. The <a href="https://agefriendly.osu.edu/cdn/Extreme-Weather-and-Older-Adults-Service-Coordinator-Toolkit-9.2025-1.pdf">tool kit we created</a> can help social service providers prepare low-income residents for extreme weather.</p>

<p>Our team is now working with service providers nationwide to document best practices, identify gaps and ensure residents are better prepared for climate- and weather-related emergencies in the future.</p>

body: Heavy rain inundated already saturated yards in Hollywood, Fla., south of Fort Lauderdale, on Nov. 18, 2026
Joe Raedle/Getty Images Floodwater filled the streets and crept into homes across Florida’s Atlantic coast as an intense storm dumped more than a foot of rain in 24 hours starting Nov. 17, 2026
The deluge followed extreme downpours in parts of the region less than three weeks earlier , and forecasters warned of more rain still to come
As people in Fort Lauderdale watched the water rise in their already saturated yards, it may have felt like déjà vu
In April 2023, more than 25 inches of rain fell in Fort Lauderdale in 24 hours
Even hurricanes rarely drop that much rain in one area that fast
Residents could do little to stop the flooding
Studies show that as global temperatures rise, more people will be at risk from such destructive flooding – including in areas that rarely faced extreme flooding in the past

In many of these communities, the people at greatest risk of harm from flash flooding are low-wage workers , older adults and other vulnerable residents who live in low-lying areas and who have few resources to protect their properties and themselves
I study the impact of extreme weather on vulnerable communities as an associate professor of social work
To limit the damage, communities need to know who is at risk and how they can be better prepared
More extreme downpours in a warming world The Florida storms offer a view into the risks ahead as temperatures rise
These risks are especially high as the effects of a strong 2026-27 El Niño set in
A warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture , leading to stronger downpours
These events are expected to increase in frequency and intensity in many regions as greenhouse gas emissions from human activities continue to heat up the planet
Where extreme precipitation events are forecast to increase under a low-emissions scenario and a high one
National Climate Assessment 2018 Recent disasters show how the risk of flash flooding is expanding beyond areas traditionally considered at risk
Knowing who is most at risk To plan for extreme weather, it’s crucial for community leaders and residents to know where the risks are highest and who might not be prepared
Low-lying areas with poorly planned development , lack of investment in protective infrastructure and the lingering effects of historic disinvestment and discrimination are often at higher risk
So are low-income communities with tight budgets that can’t afford protective measures like upgraded levees or stormwater systems and can’t recover from damage quickly
When older adults live in these flood-prone areas , they are at even higher risk
Older adults have a higher likelihood of having health needs or some form of disability that could affect their ability to leave quickly during a disaster
They are also more likely to be socially isolated , which may mean they don’t hear timely information or have help to evacuate or quick access to resources for recovering
Residents walk out of a flooded neighborhood in Fort Lauderdale, Fla., with their pet on April 13, 2023

Joe Raedle/Getty Images Renters and the impact of housing insecurity My colleagues and I have examined how prepared people are for disasters of any kind across the U.S. – flooding, tornadoes, hurricanes and others – and how housing security played a role

Overall, we found in a 2023 study that 57% of the population, among 29,070 housing units surveyed nationwide, reported they were not prepared with food, water, emergency funds and transportation in case disaster struck

We found that households facing housing insecurity – those behind on their payments for rent, mortgage or utilities – were less prepared for disasters than others, even when the occupants had similar incomes and education
For residents with low incomes and without flood insurance, cleanup costs from flooding can be overwhelming
Joe Raedle/Getty Images People who are struggling to meet day-to-day needs often don’t have the ability and resources to plan for everyday events, let alone for disasters
Our research has shown that households with children, households led by women, and low-income households were less prepared than others for disasters
In the U.S., lower-income families often depend on the rental market
They tend to move more frequently, and since they don’t own the property, they often can’t make upgrades for safety
And landlords might not prioritize those risks that seem rare but carry costs
How to help communities stay safe The most effective way to address these challenges is through solutions that are tailored to the community

That can involve investing in infrastructure , including state-funded priorities such as drainage systems, large-scale flood prevention measures and strengthening the power grid , as well as ensuring that people have access to safe and affordable housing
Some communities and federal agencies have bought out properties that frequently flood and changed zoning rules to prevent more people from moving into harm’s way
People walked in flooded roads in Riviera Beach, Fla., on Election Day 2026 near a polling place that had to be relocated because of the first round of November’s severe floods

Saul Martinez/Getty Images Raising community awareness about climate change and extreme weather risks is also crucial, especially among those most at risk , such as older adults and other socially marginalized groups

If people understand the risks, know how to prepare their homes, know how to plan for emergencies , know whom to contact for help, and have stronger systems of care, they’re more likely to be prepared when disasters strike

title: A convincing vegan meat alternative needs both taste and texture – here’s how food scientists manufacture them

<title>A convincing vegan meat alternative needs both taste and texture – here’s how food scientists manufacture them</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771922/original/file-20261113-64-yaivej.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=375%2C0%2C4050%2C2700&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Plant-based burger patties are designed to offer an alternative to conventional meat, using plant-derived ingredients to recreate familiar textures and flavors. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/closeup-of-young-asian-women-friends-hold-knife-royalty-free-image/1497918288">MTStock Studio/E+ via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>This Thanksgiving, you may sit down to a table laden with mashed potatoes, cranberry sauce, vegetables and a golden-brown turkey. And, if you have any vegetarians or vegans in your family, you may even see a plant-based meat alternative. But how do food scientists make something taste and look similar to turkey entirely from plants?</p>

<p>Plant-based meat alternatives have become an <a href="https://gfi.org/resource/plant-based-meat-eggs-and-dairy-state-of-the-industry/">increasingly prominent part of the food industry</a>, driven partly by concerns about the sustainability of conventional meat production and the search for additional protein sources. One life-cycle assessment found that plant-based patties had a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.spc.2021.07.017">77% lower climate impact</a> than the Brazilian beef patties examined, although the results varied depending on the production systems and environmental measures considered.</p>

<p>But making a convincing meat alternative is not as simple as replacing animal protein with plant protein. How do you turn ingredients from peas, soybeans or wheat into something that looks, tastes and feels like meat? </p>

<h2>Plants have protein, too</h2>

<p>When people think about protein, foods such as chicken, beef, eggs and milk often come to mind. However, plants are also important <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-a-protein-a-biologist-explains-152870">sources of protein</a>. Soybeans, peas, wheat, lentils and other legumes contain proteins that can be extracted and used in food products.</p>

<p>Soy and pea proteins are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.fufo.2023.100248">widely used in plant-based meat alternatives</a>. <a href="https://theconversation.com/thank-glutens-complex-chemistry-for-your-light-fluffy-baked-goods-216869">Wheat protein, or gluten</a>, can also contribute to their structure and chewy texture. Researchers are also exploring other sources, including fava beans and mung beans, to expand the range of ingredients available.</p>

<p>But plant proteins behave differently. Some absorb more water, while others <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fnut.2022.1044024">bind fat or form structures</a> that hold ingredients together. These properties influence how a food feels when you bite into it. Choosing a protein therefore involves understanding how it behaves during processing, not just its nutritional value.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772591/original/file-20261117-64-4oej9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A plate on a festive tablecloth with vegetables and a plant based turkey, which looks kind of like a meatloaf with a hollow center." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772591/original/file-20261117-64-4oej9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772591/original/file-20261117-64-4oej9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772591/original/file-20261117-64-4oej9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772591/original/file-20261117-64-4oej9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772591/original/file-20261117-64-4oej9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772591/original/file-20261117-64-4oej9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772591/original/file-20261117-64-4oej9e.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Tofurky is a common vegan turkey alternative many people serve at Thanksgiving.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/vegan-tofu-turkey-royalty-free-image/893093700?phrase=tofurkey&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">JasonOndreicka/iStock via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Why is making meat from plants so difficult?</h2>

<p>Think about biting into a piece of roasted turkey breast. Its <a href="https://doi.org/10.1155/2016/3182746">texture comes from the arrangement of muscle fibers</a>, along with connective tissue, water and fat. Together, these components create firmness, juiciness and the chewing experience you associate with meat.</p>

<p>Plant proteins have structures that are different from animal muscle proteins. Mixing pea or soy protein with water does not automatically create meatlike fibers. Food scientists use processing methods that organize these proteins into structures that more closely resemble muscle.</p>

<p>Flavor matters, too. Fat adds juiciness and carries flavor compounds, while heating creates familiar roasted and savory aromas. A convincing meat alternative must bring together the right ingredients and processing conditions to reproduce these qualities.</p>

<h2>Turning plant proteins into meatlike foods</h2>

<p>One <a href="https://www.ift.org/food-technology-magazine/how-extrusion-shapes-food-processing">widely used method is extrusion</a>. Protein-rich ingredients are mixed with water and pushed through a machine that applies heat and pressure while mixing the material. These forces unfold the proteins and help them interact. </p>

<p>As the mixture cools, the proteins form aligned, fibrous structures that resemble some features of meat. High-moisture extrusion uses more water during processing, which produces fibrous products with a more meatlike texture.</p>

<p>The final structure depends on factors such as the protein source, moisture content, temperature and processing conditions. These factors influence how proteins interact and form the fibrous structures <a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-food-072023-034346">found in plant-based meat alternatives</a>. </p>

<p>Manufacturers can also add fats, starches, flavorings and other ingredients to improve the eating experience. Small changes in formulation or processing can make a considerable difference, affecting whether a product is firmer, softer, chewier or better at retaining moisture.</p>

<h2>A potential future for meat alternatives</h2>

<p>Another emerging approach is 3D food printing. Like a <a href="https://3dprinting.com/what-is-3d-printing/">conventional 3D printer</a>, a food printer builds an object layer by layer, <a href="https://www.zmescience.com/science/news-science/3d-printed-food-is-coming-to-a-grocery-store-near-you-and-you-might-not-even-notice/">depositing edible materials</a> according to a digital design.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771924/original/file-20261113-64-hq7yyq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Three beakers full of plant-based foods, and two dishes of imitation meat made from those foods." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771924/original/file-20261113-64-hq7yyq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771924/original/file-20261113-64-hq7yyq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771924/original/file-20261113-64-hq7yyq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771924/original/file-20261113-64-hq7yyq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771924/original/file-20261113-64-hq7yyq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771924/original/file-20261113-64-hq7yyq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771924/original/file-20261113-64-hq7yyq.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Researchers and food companies are exploring 3D printing to create new textures and structures in meat alternatives.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/printed-vegetarian-products-that-imitate-prepared-meat-are-news-photo/2231729377">Emmanuele Contini/NurPhoto via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p><a href="https://stories.wvu.edu/whats-cooking">Our research explores</a> protein-based food inks: mixtures designed to flow through a printer nozzle and hold their shape once deposited. Developing the right formulation is challenging because the material must be fluid enough to print but still firm enough to retain its shape. Researchers are applying similar principles to explore printing plant-based meat alternatives.</p>

<p>Instead of relying only on conventional manufacturing methods, 3D printing could allow researchers to control how different ingredients are arranged. For example, you could potentially deposit protein-rich materials and fat-containing ingredients in specific patterns to create different structures and textures.</p>

<p>Recent research on <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.foodchem.2025.144157">the 3D-printing of plant-protein-based meat analogs</a> highlights how the formulation of the food ink and printing conditions influence how accurately a product can be printed and whether it holds its shape. However, a printed product that looks like meat must still deliver the expected texture, flavor and eating experience.</p>

<p>Plant-based meat alternatives are not necessarily intended to replace traditional meat. They offer consumers additional choices, but making them appealing, affordable and consistent remains a challenge. Scientists continue to study how proteins, ingredients and processing work together to create the textures and flavors people enjoy.</p>

<p>The next time you see a plant-based burger or turkey alternative, remember that making it involves much more than replacing animal protein with plant protein. Technologies such as extrusion and 3D food printing are helping scientists explore new ways to turn plant ingredients into meatlike foods.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296038/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Today’s Thanksgiving holiday was invented amid the Civil War to unite a divided country

<title>Today’s Thanksgiving holiday was invented amid the Civil War to unite a divided country</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772029/original/file-20261115-64-ja2ftm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C700%2C466&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Sarah Josepha Hale&#39;s September 1863 letter to President Abraham Lincoln, petitioning for a national Thanksgiving holiday</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Letter-SarahHaletoLincoln.jpg">Library of Congress via Wikimedia Commons</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving. Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England’s first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God’s providence.</p>

<p>Children learn the story as if it were history – and as though Americans have commemorated Thanksgiving the same way ever since. The only existing <a href="https://plimoth.org/yath/unit-4/eye-witness-account-of-the-1621-harvest-celebration">eyewitness account</a> of this event does not, however, say much about what was eaten. <a href="https://plimoth.org/yath/unit-4/excerpt-from-william-bradfords-of-plymouth-plantation-harvest-of-1621">A slightly later account</a> of the 1621 harvest mentions seasonal food such as venison, corn – and, yes, turkeys.</p>

<p>The idea of a straight line connecting <a href="https://theconversation.com/where-are-the-voices-of-indigenous-peoples-in-the-thanksgiving-story-51089">that “first Thanksgiving</a>” to Thanksgivings today is, in fact, an American myth. It is a story created in the 19th century <a href="https://visit.archives.gov/whats-on/explore-exhibits/president-abraham-lincolns-thanksgiving-day-proclamation">to unify a nation</a> and long used to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/0308275X9201200205">assimilate new immigrants</a> into it.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">

<h2>Creating today’s Thanksgiving</h2>

<p>The Pilgrims and Puritans, who started arriving in Massachusetts shortly afterward, <a href="https://divinity.uchicago.edu/sightings/articles/thanksgiving-day-remember-fast-day-dean-grodzins">regularly held fasts and feasts</a>. On fast days, the community atoned for sins they believed they had committed. On feast days, they gave thanks to God. Some governors of colonies – and later, states – <a href="https://www.si.edu/spotlight/thanksgiving/history">declared fall holidays of thanksgiving</a>, but did not coordinate with each other.</p>

<p>The Thanksgiving that we know, with the traditional recipes and the close connection to the Pilgrims, was largely the creation of one woman: <a href="https://www.womenshistory.org/education-resources/biographies/sarah-hale">Sarah Josepha Hale</a>, who was born in New Hampshire in 1788. In the 1830s she became the editor of <a href="https://www.nysoclib.org/blog/special-collections-highlight-godeys-ladys-book-sarah-josepha-hale-and-american-culture">Godey’s Lady’s’ Book</a>, which had the largest circulation of any U.S. magazine before the Civil War.</p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771745/original/file-20261112-64-jxuju7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A faded cover page of a magazine, with black and white illustrations of flowers, women and children." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771745/original/file-20261112-64-jxuju7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/771745/original/file-20261112-64-jxuju7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=915&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771745/original/file-20261112-64-jxuju7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=915&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771745/original/file-20261112-64-jxuju7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=915&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771745/original/file-20261112-64-jxuju7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1149&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771745/original/file-20261112-64-jxuju7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1149&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/771745/original/file-20261112-64-jxuju7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1149&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<p>Godey’s included clothing patterns, recipes, articles on home management, essays on educating children, recipes and fiction. Hale believed that the woman was the heart of the home and responsible for creating an upstanding, God-fearing, wholesome family.</p>

<p>She was also deeply committed to her young country and believed that homemakers could help create its national identity. According to historian <a href="https://history.illinois.edu/directory/profile/epleck">Elizabeth Pleck</a>, Hale began publishing editorials <a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674002791">calling for a national Thanksgiving</a>, along with instructions for what the day could look like.</p>

<p>Godey’s taught readers how to celebrate the day, with recipes for seasonal food such as turkey and cranberry sauce. The centerpiece of the table was the pies, which featured elaborate pastry decorations: the Mayflower or a cornucopia, created out of pie crust. The full table was a celebration of “women’s work,” at a time when the Industrial Revolution was <a href="https://www.uml.edu/tsongas/barilla-taylor/women-industrial-revolution.aspx">shifting the economy toward factories and other business</a>, making the importance of unpaid domestic labor less obvious.</p>

<p>Hale’s idea of Thanksgiving also emphasized returning to loved ones, as those factories were drawing many workers away from home. She saw it as a day to tell family stories – and the story of the nation, starting with the first Thanksgiving. </p>

<p>Hale <a href="https://www.whitehousehistory.org/press-room/press-timelines/thanksgiving-at-the-white-house">petitioned five presidents</a> to declare Thanksgiving a national holiday. Abraham Lincoln finally took her up on it, hoping that a national holiday emphasizing the country’s origin story would prove uniting during the Civil War. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772031/original/file-20261115-64-fld0gn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A faded illustration in black ink of three men in soldiers' uniforms breaking a small bone between them." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772031/original/file-20261115-64-fld0gn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772031/original/file-20261115-64-fld0gn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772031/original/file-20261115-64-fld0gn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772031/original/file-20261115-64-fld0gn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=398&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772031/original/file-20261115-64-fld0gn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=500&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772031/original/file-20261115-64-fld0gn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=500&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/772031/original/file-20261115-64-fld0gn.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=500&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<p>Northern women sent pies to the families of soldiers and turkeys to the men at the front. Pleck notes that abolitionist <a href="https://www.womenshistory.org/education-resources/biographies/sojourner-truth">Sojourner Truth</a> <a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674002791">went door to door</a>, collecting funds to provide Thanksgiving dinners to African American troops. </p>

<p>The holiday <a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674002791">caught on gradually</a>. Given the Protestant origins of early Americans’ feast and fast days, Catholics were slow to embrace it. Given its association with Lincoln and the war, the South was also late to adopt it. And given the day’s emphasis on family, it was less celebrated on the frontier, where single men dominated. </p>

<p>Wherever Thanksgiving was celebrated, however, Godey’s Lady’s Book taught Americans how to celebrate it. The magazine’s op-eds connected the holiday menu and the past, using the Pilgrims’ courage to inspire 19th-century Americans dealing with massive changes in their own lives: war, industrialization, urbanization and the frontier. </p>

<h2>Assimilating immigrants</h2>

<p>Before long, Thanksgiving was also seen as a way to assimilate immigrants. </p>

<p>This vision was, in part, popularized by political cartoonist <a href="https://www.illustrationhistory.org/artists/thomas-nast">Thomas Nast</a>. “<a href="https://www.nyhistory.org/blogs/uncle-sams-thanksgiving-dinner-thomas-nasts-powerful">Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner</a>,” which appeared in Harper’s Weekly in 1869, depicted Americans from any number of races and ethnicities in their national dress: men, women and children sitting as equals around a dinner table, with portraits of presidents on the wall, while Uncle Sam carved a turkey.</p>

<p>The image suggested that immigrants could be incorporated into the nation – and formerly enslaved people, too. It was printed just one year after <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-14/">the 14th Amendment</a> granted citizenship to anyone born in the U.S. and four years after the <a href="https://constitution.congress.gov/constitution/amendment-13/">13th Amendment</a> formally ended slavery.</p>

<p>Nast’s image contrasted sharply to another cartoon, also called “<a href="https://www.researchgate.net/figure/Uncle-Sams-Thanksgiving-Dinner-by-George-Frederick-Keller_fig1_313536819">Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner</a>,” that G.F. Keller drew for the San Francisco Wasp eight years later. Keller’s disheveled and entirely male collection of diners each ate their own national food, or offensive stereotypes thereof, suggesting immigrants could never truly become American. </p>

<p>But many Americans believed they could – although they demanded most immigrants give up their “Old World ways” and take on customs of their new country. Thanksgiving was part of the engine of that assimilation. </p>

<p>In the early 20th century, public schools taught about Thanksgiving and sent children home with recipe cards so that their parents could cook the same kinds of recipes Hale had popularized in the previous century. Schools framed the Pilgrims and their first Thanksgiving as the spiritual, if not literal, ancestors of all Americans: the first “immigrants.” They didn’t dwell on how the Pilgrims’ arrival <a href="https://theconversation.com/thanksgiving-stories-gloss-over-the-history-of-us-settlement-on-native-lands-213517">looked more like colonization</a> than immigration. </p>

<p>The holiday became a way to include newcomers in the national myth. By the 1920s, in fact, Thanksgiving was <a href="https://time.com/5725168/thanksgiving-history-lesson/">the most celebrated holiday</a> <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/roomfordebate/2015/11/25/rethinking-the-way-we-teach-thanksgiving/does-thanksgiving-even-belong-in-schools">in public schools</a>. Pleck quotes one Jewish immigrant reflecting on his childhood and saying the Pilgrims were a way to connect  “us offspring of Jewish immigrants – our own exiled fathers who had crossed the seas – <a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674002791">and the traditions of Protestant America</a>.” Students acted out the first Thanksgiving and were told they belonged to a “nation of immigrants.” </p>

<p>While some immigrant parents rejected the holiday, others embraced it, with spins to make it their own. Many served a turkey surrounded by the celebratory dishes of their own cultures. For Jews, the early 1900s <a href="https://mjhnyc.org/blog/crisco-and-the-jewish-american-cook/">invention of Crisco</a> <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-crisco-toppled-lard-and-made-americans-believers-in-industrial-food-127158">as a nondairy butter substitute</a> allowed them to create a truly “American” Thanksgiving and dessert, without violating kosher rules against mixing meat and milk.</p>

<p>The fact that most families celebrate at home allowed immigrants and their children to take part in the national culture, while still expressing their own. During my own New England childhood, an Indian neighbor had my mother’s fairly classic cranberry relish, and by the end of the weekend she’d worked out a cranberry chutney with Indian spices. When we had Thankgiving dinner with my parents’ friends the Stalzmans, who were Jewish, matzah ball soup was the opening course.</p>

<p>At times, the idea of the Pilgrims arriving on the Mayflower <a href="https://www.axios.com/2024/11/27/first-thanksgiving-history-pilgrims">has been used to exclude</a> – to imply that only Americans <a href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/1985/09/05/mayflower-descendants-a-breed-apart/">whose literal ancestors came over on the ship</a>, and other white Protestants like them, truly belong. Yet on the holiday in their memory, generations of new Americans affirmed that they, too, belonged.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/289016/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: Sarah Josepha Hale's September 1863 letter to President Abraham Lincoln, petitioning for a national Thanksgiving holiday Library of Congress via Wikimedia Commons It is hard to imagine a more American holiday than Thanksgiving

Every year, elementary schoolers learn about the first celebration: that after surviving a terrible year, New England’s first European immigrants, the Pilgrims, invited their Indigenous neighbors to a feast in gratitude for their help and God’s providence
Children learn the story as if it were history – and as though Americans have commemorated Thanksgiving the same way ever since
The only existing eyewitness account of this event does not, however, say much about what was eaten
A slightly later account of the 1621 harvest mentions seasonal food such as venison, corn – and, yes, turkeys
The idea of a straight line connecting that “first Thanksgiving ” to Thanksgivings today is, in fact, an American myth
It is a story created in the 19th century to unify a nation and long used to assimilate new immigrants into it
Immigrants celebrate Thanksgiving at The Cambodian Family, an organization in Santa Ana, Calif., in 2002
Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images Creating today’s Thanksgiving The Pilgrims and Puritans, who started arriving in Massachusetts shortly afterward, regularly held fasts and feasts
On fast days, the community atoned for sins they believed they had committed
Some governors of colonies – and later, states – declared fall holidays of thanksgiving , but did not coordinate with each other
The Thanksgiving that we know, with the traditional recipes and the close connection to the Pilgrims, was largely the creation of one woman: Sarah Josepha Hale , who was born in New Hampshire in 1788
In the 1830s she became the editor of Godey’s Lady’s’ Book , which had the largest circulation of any U.S. magazine before the Civil War
Before the Civil War, Godey’s had the largest magazine circulation in the United States
Wikimedia Commons Godey’s included clothing patterns, recipes, articles on home management, essays on educating children, recipes and fiction
Hale believed that the woman was the heart of the home and responsible for creating an upstanding, God-fearing, wholesome family
She was also deeply committed to her young country and believed that homemakers could help create its national identity
According to historian Elizabeth Pleck , Hale began publishing editorials calling for a national Thanksgiving , along with instructions for what the day could look like
Godey’s taught readers how to celebrate the day, with recipes for seasonal food such as turkey and cranberry sauce
The centerpiece of the table was the pies, which featured elaborate pastry decorations: the Mayflower or a cornucopia, created out of pie crust

The full table was a celebration of “women’s work,” at a time when the Industrial Revolution was shifting the economy toward factories and other business , making the importance of unpaid domestic labor less obvious
Hale’s idea of Thanksgiving also emphasized returning to loved ones, as those factories were drawing many workers away from home
She saw it as a day to tell family stories – and the story of the nation, starting with the first Thanksgiving
Hale petitioned five presidents to declare Thanksgiving a national holiday

Abraham Lincoln finally took her up on it, hoping that a national holiday emphasizing the country’s origin story would prove uniting during the Civil War. ‘Thanksgiving Day in the Army – After Dinner, The Wish Bone,’ by Winslow Homer, appeared in Harper’s Weekly in 1964
Metropolitan Museum of Art via Wikimedia Commons Northern women sent pies to the families of soldiers and turkeys to the men at the front
Pleck notes that abolitionist Sojourner Truth went door to door , collecting funds to provide Thanksgiving dinners to African American troops
Given the Protestant origins of early Americans’ feast and fast days, Catholics were slow to embrace it
Given its association with Lincoln and the war, the South was also late to adopt it
And given the day’s emphasis on family, it was less celebrated on the frontier, where single men dominated
Wherever Thanksgiving was celebrated, however, Godey’s Lady’s Book taught Americans how to celebrate it

The magazine’s op-eds connected the holiday menu and the past, using the Pilgrims’ courage to inspire 19th-century Americans dealing with massive changes in their own lives: war, industrialization, urbanization and the frontier
Assimilating immigrants Before long, Thanksgiving was also seen as a way to assimilate immigrants

This vision was, in part, popularized by political cartoonist Thomas Nast . “ Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner ,” which appeared in Harper’s Weekly in 1869, depicted Americans from any number of races and ethnicities in their national dress: men, women and children sitting as equals around a dinner table, with portraits of presidents on the wall, while Uncle Sam carved a turkey. ‘Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner,’ by Thomas Nast, appeared in Harper’s Weekly in 1869
Harper's Weekly via Wikimedia Commons The image suggested that immigrants could be incorporated into the nation – and formerly enslaved people, too
It was printed just one year after the 14th Amendment granted citizenship to anyone born in the U.S. and four years after the 13th Amendment formally ended slavery
Nast’s image contrasted sharply to another cartoon, also called “ Uncle Sam’s Thanksgiving Dinner ,” that G.F
Keller drew for the San Francisco Wasp eight years later
Keller’s disheveled and entirely male collection of diners each ate their own national food, or offensive stereotypes thereof, suggesting immigrants could never truly become American
But many Americans believed they could – although they demanded most immigrants give up their “Old World ways” and take on customs of their new country

<title>How the US power rivalry with Russia and China is turning outer space into the next battlefront</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772261/original/file-20261116-79-142lyg.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=509%2C0%2C5151%2C3432&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">The Air Force secretary&#39;s recent announcement that the U.S. has weapons deployed in Earth&#39;s orbit marks the first time a space power has acknowledged a role in space weaponization. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/global-security-crisis-concept-with-military-royalty-free-image/2265191660?phrase=US%20weapons%20space&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Vithun Khamsong/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>U.S. Air Force Secretary Troy Meink recently confirmed that <a href="https://abcnews.com/Politics/air-force-secretary-acknowledges-us-weapons-space/story?id=136437923">the United States has weapons deployed in Earth’s orbit</a>. To date, the <a href="https://www.spaceforce.mil/about-us/">U.S. Space Force</a>, the space service branch of the U.S. armed forces, has provided <a href="https://www.spaceforce.mil/News/Article-Display/Article/4601219/secaf-announces-on-orbit-space-control-weapons/">relatively few details</a> about what these weapons are or what they can do except that they are what Meink called “on-orbit space control weapons.”</p>

<p>Meink’s announcement is significant, but not necessarily because the U.S. is the first country to place weapons in orbit. For years, <a href="https://www.clickorlando.com/news/space-news/2026/09/21/us-military-publicly-acknowledges-it-has-weapons-in-space/">the U.S., Russia and China have accused each other</a> of developing and testing such capabilities, although none has publicly acknowledged deploying space weapons – until now.</p>

<p>We are <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=YnVdvEYAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">scholars of space law</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=YtgRGx0AAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=sra">governance</a>, and <a href="https://ostromworkshop.indiana.edu/research/space-governance/index.html">our research illustrates</a> the challenges of uniting diverse groups to establish norms related to the use of resources, safety zones and conflict prevention in new domains such as space. Without better communication and deeper coordination between the world’s space powers, we could witness the beginning of a space arms race.</p>

<h2>Failed attempts to prevent a space arms race</h2>

<p>In 1981, the <a href="https://www.unoosa.org/pdf/gares/ARES_39_59E.pdf">United Nations added</a> the Prevention of an Arms Race in Outer Space, known as <a href="https://digitallibrary.un.org/record/3895439?ln=en">PAROS</a>, to its agenda. </p>

<p>More than four decades of diplomatic efforts under PAROS have <a href="https://scholarship.law.slu.edu/lj/vol70/iss2/8/">produced meager results</a>, though there was a <a href="https://www.swfound.org/publications-and-reports/multilateral-space-security-initiatives">United Nations agreement in 2024</a> that made progress on reducing threats.</p>

<p>Despite many <a href="https://scholarship.law.slu.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=2468&amp;context=lj">countries’ proclamations supporting space arms control</a>, no multilateral treaty banning weapons in space has been adopted. With <a href="https://thegsinsight.com/arms-control-in-retreat-how-populism-and-great-power-politics-are-rewriting-global-disarmament-norms/">global arms control generally in retreat</a>, and the apparent lack of political will among the three major space powers, efforts to control space weapons have reached an impasse. </p>

<p>The question increasingly is not whether an arms race in space can be prevented, but how it will be managed.</p>

<h2>Ambiguities allow weaponization</h2>

<p><a href="https://2009-2017.state.gov/t/isn/5181.htm">The Outer Space Treaty of 1967</a>, to which all major space powers are parties, is often described by scholars, practitioners and policymakers as the constitution of outer space. </p>

<p><a href="https://2009-2017.state.gov/t/isn/5181.htm">Article IV of the treaty</a> remains the only legally binding international provision specifically regulating weapons in outer space. The article prohibits countries from placing nuclear weapons or other weapons of mass destruction in orbit around Earth. It also imposes a broader prohibition on military activities on the Moon and other celestial bodies, including establishing military bases, testing weapons and conducting military maneuvers. </p>

<p>However, the article does not prohibit conventional weapons in Earth’s orbit. That omission is significant. The treaty can be understood as <a href="https://www.armscontrol.org/factsheets/outer-space-treaty-glance">implicitly permitting what it does not prohibit</a>: the placement of such weapons in orbit.</p>

<p>China has used these ambiguities as cover for its own space weaponization efforts. In a 2007 test, <a href="https://www.cfr.org/backgrounders/chinas-anti-satellite-test">China destroyed one of its own satellites</a> while in orbit, and it has recently <a href="https://www.space.com/space-exploration/launches-spacecraft/chinas-secretive-space-plane-caught-on-camera-in-incredible-new-photo-released-by-us-military">deployed a mysterious space plane</a>. </p>

<p>China, nonetheless, <a href="https://www.wsj.com/politics/national-security/u-s-eyes-china-and-russia-as-pentagon-confirms-space-weapons-2e373e47">reacted critically</a> to the recent U.S. weapons announcement. In September 2026, it urged Washington to <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/world/asia/china-warns-us-space-weapons-fuel-arms-race-rcna598070">stop expanding its military presence in space</a>. That same month, Russia renewed calls for <a href="https://www.reuters.com/business/aerospace-defense/russia-says-there-is-still-time-stop-an-arms-race-space-after-us-orbital-weapons-2026-09-16/">the demilitarization of outer space</a>. </p>

<p>Both countries have long advocated stronger international restrictions on space weapons. Russia and China twice <a href="https://apnews.com/article/nuclear-arms-space-un-russia-us-japan-561ab8ae569afd7ee79789588ca34033">jointly proposed a treaty</a> prohibiting <a href="https://www.globaltimes.cn/page/202610/1372769.shtml">the placement of weapons in outer space</a>. <a href="https://spacenews.com/41842us-dismisses-space-weapons-treaty-proposal-as-fundamentally-flawed/">The U.S. opposed the proposals</a> in 2014, pointing to their failure to also cover important ground-based, anti-satellite weapons.</p>

<p>But Russian and Chinese declarations in favor of keeping weapons out of space sit uneasily alongside their own activities. </p>

            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink, right, announced in September 2026 that the U.S. has weapons stationed in Earth’s orbit.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/secretary-of-war-pete-hegseth-shakes-hands-with-secretary-news-photo/2300199142?phrase=Air%20Force%20Secretary%20Troy%20Meink&amp;adppopup=true">Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In 2020, U.S. Space Command, part of the Defense Department, <a href="https://www.npr.org/2020/07/23/894905696/u-s-space-force-accuses-russia-of-in-orbit-testing-of-anti-satellite-weapon">accused Russia of testing a space-based anti-satellite weapon</a> after an orbiting Russian satellite released a projectile. <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/world/u-s-accuses-russia-of-testing-anti-satellite-weapon-in-space">Russia said the spacecraft</a> was performing an inspection mission.</p>

<p>In 2024, the United States said Russia had launched another satellite, Cosmos 2576, which it assessed to be a “counter space” weapon <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cq55ww5j7e2o">capable of attacking other satellites</a>.</p>

<p>China has similarly demonstrated increasingly sophisticated operations in orbit. Five Chinese spacecraft conducted satellite flybys in 2024, an exercise that <a href="https://www.space.com/space-exploration/satellites/us-military-practices-orbital-dogfighting-in-1st-ever-live-fly-exercise-in-space">a senior U.S. Space Force officer later described</a> as practicing “dogfighting in space.”</p>

<p>None of this proves that every suspicious Russian or Chinese spacecraft is a weapon. Many technologies used for servicing, inspection and maneuvering around satellites are inherently dual-use. But it does put Moscow’s and Beijing’s calls to keep weapons out of space in perspective.</p>

<p>It also illustrates the security threat now taking shape. Washington can point to Russian and Chinese activities to justify its own weapons. Moscow and Beijing can now point to acknowledged U.S. weapons to help justify their actions, which could result in a self-fulfilling prophecy.</p>

<h2>War in space</h2>

<p>Space has been part of warfare for decades. The 1991 Gulf War has sometimes been called the first “space war” because of <a href="https://media.defense.gov/2017/Dec/29/2001861991/-1/1/0/T_KELLY_CENTRALIZED_CONTOL_OF_SPACE.PDF">the unprecedented role satellites played</a> in navigation, communications, intelligence and targeting. But satellites primarily supported military operations taking place on the ground.</p>

<p>That distinction has gradually eroded. NATO formally recognized space as <a href="https://www.nato.int/en/what-we-do/deterrence-and-defence/natos-approach-to-space">a military theater in 2019</a>. </p>

<p>Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine then demonstrated something different, in which the very definition of a weapon was challenged. </p>

<p>Hours before Russian troops crossed the border, <a href="https://www.technologyreview.com/2022/05/10/1051973/russia-hack-viasat-satellite-ukraine-invasion/">a cyberattack disrupted the U.S. satellite network Viasat</a>, in what was <a href="https://www.cigionline.org/publications/the-first-space-cyber-war-and-the-need-for-new-regimes-and-policies/">dubbed by commentators</a> as the first “<a href="https://www.cigionline.org/publications/the-first-space-cyber-war-and-the-need-for-new-regimes-and-policies/">space-cyber war</a>.” Space-based services were no longer merely supporting military operations but were themselves deliberately targeted as part of a military campaign.</p>

<p>The acknowledgment of weapons in orbit represents another step in that evolution. Space assets are transitioning from systems that primarily support warfare in other domains to systems that can be weapons, targets and participants in combat and are often replete with <a href="https://www.lse.ac.uk/ideas/projects/space-policy/publications/cyberattacks-on-satellites">vulnerabilities</a> that could be exploited by an adversary. </p>

<p>That does not mean future space warfare will resemble Star Wars dogfights or Starfleet armadas taking on Borg cubes. But the emerging battlefield is likely to be much more complicated. Satellites can be disrupted through jamming and spoofing, disabled through cyberattacks, approached or manipulated by other spacecraft, attacked from Earth or potentially attacked by weapons already in orbit.</p>

<p>This makes the connection between space and cyberspace particularly important. A country seeking to neutralize an adversary’s satellites may have several options, ranging from a cyberattack or electronic interference to physically damaging it. At the same time, space-based critical infrastructure has never been more <a href="https://www.oecd.org/en/publications/the-space-economy-at-a-glance-2026_cbf9b240-en.html">vital</a> to the functioning of the global economy.</p>

<p>Military strategy therefore has to adapt not merely to warfare in space but to warfare across an increasingly interconnected <a href="https://digitalcommons.law.uga.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1617&amp;context=glr">space-cyber nexus</a>.</p>

<h2>An arms race that must now be managed</h2>

<p>The important question is no longer whether space will become militarized. It has been militarized for decades. Nor is it even whether states will develop weapons capable of affecting objects in space. Several already have done so.</p>

<p>The new question is how nations manage a strategic environment in which weapons are openly deployed in orbit, satellites are increasingly being targeted, and attacks can move between the space and cyber domains.</p>

<p>Public acknowledgment may itself have strategic consequences.</p>

<p>The U.S. Space Force argues that revealing the existence of its orbital weapons can strengthen deterrence by <a href="https://www.space.com/space-exploration/satellites/us-space-force-says-it-operates-weapons-in-orbit-our-aim-is-deterrence">making adversaries aware</a> that it possesses capabilities with which to respond. But transparency can also accelerate competition. </p>

<p>Russia and China can now point to U.S. weapons to justify deploying their own. The same logic and its consequences <a href="https://thebulletin.org/2026/09/the-us-acknowledged-its-space-weapons-now-it-must-build-guardrails/">animated debates during the Cold War</a>.</p>

<p>Forty-five years after the United Nations began debating the prevention of an arms race in outer space, that arms race increasingly looks less like something to prevent than something governments must learn to manage.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293414/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>The stunning transformation of the Southern Democratic Party, in one lifetime</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/772479/original/file-20261117-64-b1n0a7.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C66%2C2992%2C1994&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Mississippi Democratic Gov. Ross Barnett waves a Confederate flag before the start of an Ole Miss-Kentucky football game on Sept. 29, 1962, in Jackson, Miss.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=confederate%20flag%20mississippi&amp;mediaType=photo">AP Photo/Jim Bourdier, File</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Two of the biggest surprises of the 2026 election cycle were Democratic U.S. Senate victories in the Deep South. In addition to <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/03/us/andrews-graham-south-carolina-senate.html">Annie Andrews’ victory in South Carolina</a>, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/11/us/elections/colom-mississippi-senate-democrats.html">Scott Colom won a close contest in Mississippi</a>, a place that historian James Cobb called “<a href="https://www.amazon.com/dp/0195089138?lv=shuf&amp;channelId=500&amp;plpRedirect=mhFallback">The Most Southern Place on Earth</a>.”</p>

<p>Colom is not Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator. <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cmde1y19g19do">Two Black Republicans represented the state during Reconstruction</a>, when state legislatures still selected U.S. senators. But <a href="https://apnews.com/article/scott-colom-mississippi-senate-midterms-56c18f292a734443992f9466c3b0f346">Colom is the state’s first popularly elected Black U.S. senator</a>. He is also <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/us/democrat-scott-colom-defeats-incumbent-cindy-hyde-smith-cnn-projects-2026-11-11/">the first Democrat that Mississippians have sent to the Senate since 1982</a>.</p>

<p>It is tempting to read this change using a familiar political science term: <a href="https://www.acsu.buffalo.edu/%7Ejcampbel/documents/SSHRealignment06.pdf">party realignment</a>. But as political scientists who study <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=6P3QreQAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">political campaigns</a> and <a href="https://www.coastal.edu/academics/facultyprofiles/educationandsocialsciences/politics/drewkurlowski/">Southern politics</a>, we see an equally important transformation in the electorate – the people who can cast votes.</p>

<p>Simply put, the Democratic Party in the South was transformed from a <a href="https://www.thirteen.org/wnet/jimcrow/stories_org_democratic.html">party that defended white supremacy and Black disenfranchisement</a> into one in which <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-2508.2004.00287.x">Black voters became a central constituency</a>. The Democrats who held Mississippi’s Senate seats for the majority of the 20th century were chosen by an electorate built to exclude Black citizens. Colom was elected by a dramatically different electorate and represents a very different Democratic Party.</p>

<p>To understand the magnitude of the change in Mississippi, it helps to look at the Democrats who came before Colom, what they stood for, and the political power they wielded.</p>



<h2>Reconstruction and its end</h2>

<p>For a brief period after the Civil War, Black Mississippians exercised real political power. They were a majority of the state’s population and, with the right to vote, helped elect the state Legislature that sent <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cmde1y19g19do">Hiram Revels to the U.S. Senate in 1870 and Blanche Bruce in 1875</a>, both of them Black. </p>

<p>That period did not last. White Democrats regained control of Mississippi government in the 1870s, <a href="https://aquila.usm.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1226&amp;context=jmh">aided by political violence, intimidation and electoral fraud</a>. In 1890, <a href="https://www.mshistorynow.mdah.ms.gov/issue/mississippi-constitution-of-1890-as-originally-adopted">the state adopted a new constitution</a> that used poll taxes, literacy tests and other restrictions to systematically disfranchise Black voters. Two years after the new constitution took effect, the percentage of Black men registered to vote had fallen to just <a href="https://www.newspapers.com/article/enterprise-journal-after-43-years-repub/169396290/">5.4 percent</a>.</p>

<p>The result fundamentally changed Mississippi politics. For the next several generations, the Democratic Party dominated a political system in which most Black Mississippians had little meaningful voice. Republican electoral victories were rare. One <a href="https://www.newspapers.com/article/enterprise-journal-after-43-years-repub/169396290/">newspaper in 1963</a> claimed that the election of Lewis McAllister to the state House was the party’s first win in 43 years. Without a competitive general election, winning the Democratic primary often meant winning office, and the politicians who emerged from a one-party system made possible by Black disenfranchisement became some of the most powerful political figures in the state’s history.</p>

<p>What happened in Mississippi reflected a broader pattern across the South. In 1949, political scientist V.O. Key published his seminal study of the region, “<a href="https://utpress.org/9780870494352/southern-politics-in-state-and-nation/">Southern Politics in State and Nation</a>.” Key argued that the solid Democratic South rested on systematic disenfranchisement of Black voters. </p>

<p>The one-party system helped keep Black Southerners out of political power while allowing white Southern politicians to present a unified front against efforts to dismantle segregation and expand Black voting rights, particularly when those efforts came from the federal government. Mississippi was among the clearest examples of that system.</p>
