<h2>Segregation and political power</h2>

<p>Before Colom, the last Democrat elected to the <a href="https://bioguide.congress.gov/search/bio/S000852">U.S. Senate from Mississippi was John Stennis in 1982</a>. He first won election in 1947, filling the seat of <a href="https://www.britannica.com/biography/Theodore-G-Bilbo">Theodore Bilbo</a>, who had won reelection in 1946 after a campaign in which <a href="https://auetd.auburn.edu/bitstream/handle/10415/3040/wakefield_zach_ma_thesis_auetd_upload_resubmit_20120412.pdf?sequence=2&amp;isAllowed=y">he urged white Mississippians to keep Black voters away from the polls</a>. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1532673X7900700307">Stennis won a 1947 special election with 52,068 votes</a> in a state of 2.2 million people. He held that seat for 41 years.</p>

<p>Throughout much of his career, <a href="https://www.navytimes.com/news/your-navy/2020/06/23/john-c-stennis-was-an-ardent-segregationist-is-it-time-to-change-the-carriers-name/">Stennis was an ardent segregationist</a>. In 1956, he was one of 101 members of Congress from the South who signed what was called the “<a href="https://www.crmvet.org/docs/560312_southern_manifesto.pdf">Southern Manifesto</a>.” In that statement, these lawmakers denounced the Supreme Court’s decision in <a href="https://www.oyez.org/cases/1940-1955/347us483">Brown v. Board of Education</a>, in which the justices ruled that the “separate but equal” standards of racial segregation were unconstitutional; Stennis and the other signatories pledged resistance to school desegregation. </p>

<p>Later in his Senate career, Stennis was <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-srv/opinions/articles/solemn_senate_votes_for_national_holiday.html">the only Southern Democrat who voted to oppose</a> the creation of a national holiday honoring Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr.</p>

<p>Stennis’ Senate colleague for much of his tenure, Mississippi <a href="https://bioguide.congress.gov/search/bio/E000018?__cf_chl_tk=nSsQRKOSHVDkKItjRP1VujR16jCfSkjLRJeh0LNd3_k-1794860208-1.0.1.1-uEE9VKLsL.F29i99Rlu6ftRueSq6ObDeFuYZF.ltxJs">Democrat James Eastland</a>, was an equally staunch defender of segregation. A cotton planter from the Mississippi Delta, he was <a href="https://www.senate.gov/senators/FeaturedBios/Featured_Bio_EastlandJames.htm">appointed to the Senate in 1941 and won the seat outright in 1942</a>. He remained in the Senate until 1978. </p>

<p>The day after the Supreme Court handed down its 1954 decision in Brown v. Board of Education, <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/news/post-nation/wp/2014/05/16/how-the-washington-post-covered-brown-v-board-of-education-in-1954/">Eastland was quoted saying</a>, “the South will not abide by nor obey this legislative decision by a political court.” </p>

<p>Recent attention has understandably focused on Stennis, the last Democrat to represent Mississippi in the Senate. When Colom takes office, he will occupy the Senate seat once held by Eastland and <a href="https://bioguide.congress.gov/search/bio/v000070">Democrat James Vardaman</a>, who <a href="https://www.pbs.org/wgbh/americanexperience/features/flood-vardaman/">said that</a> “if it is necessary every Negro in the state will be lynched; it will be done to maintain white supremacy.” </p>

<p>One-party rule also gave Mississippi’s senators unusual power. With little electoral competition, they could remain in office for decades. In a Senate where seniority mattered, longevity translated into influence. </p>

<p>Eastland, for example, chaired the Senate Judiciary Committee for more than two decades, giving him enormous influence over civil rights legislation. During his chairmanship of the powerful committee, <a href="https://www.senate.gov/legislative/landmark-legislation/civil-rights.htm">that committee became known as</a> “the graveyard of civil rights legislation,” according to the Senate’s website. </p>

<h2>A new Southern coalition</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/R47520">The Voting Rights Act of 1965</a> helped dismantle the electoral system that had sustained these men in office. Before it, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199873821.001.0001">fewer than 10% of Black Mississippians were even registered to vote</a>. Within a few short years, a majority were. </p>

<p>Black voters increasingly aligned with the Democratic Party as its national leaders embraced civil rights, even while many Democratic officeholders in Mississippi continued to defend segregation. That meant <a href="https://www.npr.org/2016/08/25/491389942/when-african-american-voters-shifted-away-from-the-gop">Black voters sometimes supported incumbent white segregationists</a>. The party’s voters changed faster than many of its candidates did. </p>

<p>The 1978 election for the seat Colom will hold illustrates how complicated that transition could be. After Eastland retired, Charles Evers, brother of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/politics/1978/11/08/cochran-winning-senate-seat-in-miss/6f7c49e3-170f-44a4-a4db-c56ac05bb68e/">ran as an independent and drew nearly a quarter of the vote</a>. His candidacy split the traditionally Democratic vote, helping Republican Thad Cochran win with a mere plurality. </p>

<p>By the 21st century, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2010/11/07/us/07south.html">white Mississippians overwhelmingly supported Republican</a> candidates, and <a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674012486">Republican dominance had replaced the old Democratic dominance</a> in most statewide elections.</p>

<p>That pattern made <a href="https://www.ms.now/opinion/why-scott-colom-mississippi-senate-win-matters-2026">Colom’s victory all the more striking</a>. He won with overwhelming support from Black voters while also attracting enough white voters to build a winning statewide coalition. </p>

<p>The contrast with Mississippi’s old Democratic coalition could hardly be sharper. The Democratic Party of Vardaman, Bilbo, Eastland and Stennis maintained its power in part by keeping Black Mississippians away from the ballot box with violence and Jim Crow laws. </p>

<p>When Colom is sworn in, Revels’ old seat will, for the first time, be held by a Black senator directly elected by Mississippi voters.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/296566/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

title: Anthropic’s early birds are getting very rich
excerpt: Anthropic signage at the Morgan Stanley headquarters in New York on November 18, 2026. | Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in To
body: Anthropic signage at the Morgan Stanley headquarters in New York on November 18, 2026. | Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day.  Subscribe here
Americans have debated, derided, praised, and protested the frontier AI labs
But they’ve never been able to directly own a piece of one…until tomorrow at 9 am
That’s when Anthropic, developer of the chatbot Claude, is expected to go public at a valuation of  more than $1 trillion
That would immediately rank the almost-six-year-old lab among the world’s most valuable publicly traded companies — up there with the likes of Walmart and JPMorgan Chase

It’s a major public test of what investors think Anthropic is worth, at a moment when a  lot of people — policymakers, regulators, and technologists among them — are questioning the economic and social value of the AI industry

AI stocks have been shaky lately, and many of the new congressional Democrats have promised to take a tougher stance toward data centers and related technology.  But you wouldn’t know it from the hype around the IPO, which is on track to become one of the largest ever

Anthropic initially set a price range of $70 to $78 a share, then  reportedly revised the offering at $83 per share as demand  surged far beyond the number of shares available.  Investors are apparently betting that Anthropic has more growing to do

For ordinary buyers, that represents a chance to share in a company whose technology could cost us our jobs …if not our very existence on Earth . 💀 The biggest winners, however, will almost undoubtedly be the executives, employees, and early investors at Anthropic itself

Go a little deeper View Link Some of America’s most iconic companies went public very early in their lifecycles. (Think Apple, Amazon, and eBay, which all IPO-ed before they were five years old.) But over the past two decades or so, many of America’s biggest businesses have instead grown in private
Between the early 2000s and 2025, the  median age of a company at IPO doubled from six years in 2000 to 12 in 2025.  Analysts credit two main factors for these increasingly late-breaking IPOs
One is the fast-growing availability of private capital from venture funds, wealthy individuals, and other companies

Firms that once needed to go public to raise money to grow can now raise that money privately.  The other factor is the desire to maintain control over the company and its information: Private firms don’t have to file public financial reports or give public shareholders a vote on corporate matters.  But while that may be good for companies and their leaders, it’s not always or unambiguously great for the general public

Financial reports shed valuable light on how a business operates and where its risks lie, for instance.  There’s a financial downside for us normies, too. “The way I see it, the later a company goes public, the more of its growth gains accrue to private investors,” Brad Badertscher , a professor of accountancy at the University of Notre Dame who has studied IPO trends, said in an email to Vox
Under this system, insiders like executives, employees, and early investors can nab shares at a low price while the company is still young and then benefit if its value goes up
Retail investors only join the party after much of that growth has already happened
Early investors, private or public, also take on a lot of risk

And even now, several years in, new investors are still taking a substantial risk when they buy shares in Anthropic — a company that, in the grand scheme of recent IPOs, isn’t even that late to the process.   There’s the threat of greater regulation from a Democratic Congress

The specter of a potential AI market crash (to say nothing about the aforementioned end of the world).  If would-be shareholders are bothered, however…you’d never know it! They’ve been waiting years to buy Anthropic stock, and they very much want in.  One link for later ➨ Become a (moderately) better home cook
Especially if you’re a beginner, it’s easy to make perfect the enemy of good
But you don’t have to be a master chef to turn out a great Thanksgiving feast (…or to feel confident in the kitchen, in general!)
Buy a decent knife and stock your spice drawer

Before you go… Did you know… there’s a type of bird that quite literally sews its nest together? They’re called common tailorbirds, and they stitch leaves with spiderwebs or plant fibers after poking holes in them.  Today’s trivia: What’s the name of the US soccer player who scored the game-winning penalty kick at the 1999 Women’s World Cup? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you for the 13th-century explorer who dictated the story of his travels to his prison cellmate
That would be Marco Polo, who shared his tale with the writer Rustichello da Pisa when they were both jailed in Genoa in the late 1290s.

title: Trump’s looming nominations crunch
excerpt: Bill Cassidy (R-LA) in the US Capitol Building on November 10, 2026. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter
body: Bill Cassidy (R-LA) in the US Capitol Building on November 10, 2026. | Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here
Welcome to The Logoff: President Donald Trump is running out of time to get his nominees confirmed
What’s happening? On Wednesday, outgoing Republican Sen
Bill Cassidy blocked Trump’s nominee to lead the National Science Foundation, Jim O’Neill, from confirmation

And last night, the White House pulled another nominee, would-be FDA commissioner Heidi Overton, from consideration ahead of a Wednesday committee vote.  Both come at the worst possible time for Trump, who’s facing a dwindling legislative calendar with a Republican Senate majority on its way out.  Cassidy, a physician, chairs the Senate health committee, which is responsible for approving both nominations before they go to the full Senate

On Tuesday evening, he  wrote in a social media post that “unfortunately, with the limited time left, confirming a permanent FDA Commissioner will fall to Senate Democrats.” What’s the context? A new Congress will be sworn in on January 3, in about a month and a half, and Democrats will hold sizable majorities in both chambers

In reality, though, the Senate has less time than that to deal with new nominations: Not only are the holidays approaching, but Congress has other big-ticket priorities on its plate, including heading off another government shutdown and potential deals on permitting reform and the debt ceiling.  Why does this matter? Trump loves an acting appointment, but those officials can often only serve for so long in a role without Senate approval, which will be an uphill battle in a Senate with a 56-seat Democratic majority. (For perspective: Even with Republicans in control, some of his most controversial nominees, like Pete Hegseth and Robert F

And incoming Sen.-elect Annie Andrews (D-SC) ran on impeaching Kennedy .) The new Senate is also near certain to spell the end of Trump’s ability to confirm judges to lower courts or the Supreme Court for the remainder of his presidency.  In other words, time is of the essence and failed nominations like O’Neill and Overton are a particularly big deal
If Trump wants to fill those jobs, he’ll need to find a nominee that a new Democratic majority in the Senate is willing to confirm — I won’t be holding my breath

And with that, it’s time to log off… Here’s a useful column from Gabe Bullard, writing for Vox: Big Tech loves to use convenience as a selling point, especially in an age of AI agents that can do things like book your flights and shop for your groceries (as long as you’re willing to tolerate the possibility that something with access to your credit card can go badly awry) .  So how can we tell when these products are actually worth it, and when are they just locking us into a new set of hassles? Gabe breaks it all down here , and you can read it with a gift link
Have a great evening and we’ll see you tomorrow!

body: A traveler at Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Austin, Texas, on November 16, 2026. | Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images Last week — on Friday the 13th, of all days — everyone became hyperaware of how fragile our air infrastructure is
For four hours and 21 minutes, the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, grounding all flights
Tens of thousands of flights were impacted, even more people were stuck at airports, and theories about the cause spread like wildfire
Then the Trump administration finger-pointing began.  Eventually, however, the truth came out: The grounding wasn’t the result of a cyberattack, some kind of AI incident, or something even stranger

Instead, it was routine — though maybe ill-considered — maintenance gone awry.  Even with the mystery solved, though, the fact that so many flights were grounded over what was revealed to be a problem with a router somewhere in Arkansas is troubling the American public in a real way.  So how did it all go down? Darryl Campbell writes about aviation for The Verge, and he talked with Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram about how one router brought down the entire aviation system, why it’s likely to happen again, and what we could do to stop it
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts , Pandora , and Spotify
Did this all really happen because of a rogue router situation? It did
But don’t think about the router that you have in your house for wifi
There’s a contractor called L3Harris and they’re doing what they hope is routine maintenance on a dinky little part of the aviation infrastructure backbone for data in the middle of nowhere, Arkansas
Because they think it’s this little tiny place, they do it during the day on a Friday, which is usually not when you want to be messing with massive data infrastructure
But they think, “Well, we’re going to do it anyway.” They plug in this router for the first time
They’re basically pulling out an old telephone switch that is using copper cables and they’re installing one that has these new fiber optics
It’s super fast and all this good stuff, except that they leave a factory setting on
And the factory setting starts pinging the network hundreds of times every second.  Now, if you’re on normal new infrastructure, that’s not a problem
But the thing is the FAA’s data backbone is this kind of patchwork system of old-school technology designed in the ’50s and ’60s, with some replacements in the ’80s and ’90s

The problem is that this factory setting assumes that you’re plugging it into a brand-new system and it quickly starts overwhelming the data flow with all of these requests and kind of causing data loss in the same sense of what you would get if you’re on a FaceTime call with someone and your wifi signal isn’t very good
So you start losing bits, the audio gets a little bit choppy
Now the difference here, again, because it’s an industrial-scale thing, is that a FaceTime call doesn’t really matter if you start to lose data

But if you are tracking hundreds of flights and you need up-to-the-second audio that’s perfectly crystal clear with absolutely perfect data, once you start to lose some of that, then you can actually cause a plane crash
And so that’s something that you really, really don’t want to happen

Why is it so hard to fix these problems? The weirdest part about it all is that even though everybody flies, the timeline for doing these kinds of upgrades is really out of sync with the political timeline.  You have a major party change, a presidential change every four and eight years

But if you’re going to do a large-scale system upgrade, you literally have to be digging hundreds of miles of cables, ripping out systems, replacing them without causing the whole system to go down, for months on end
It really is a complex logistical ballet and that’s why it takes 10, 15, 20 years to do these kinds of step-change upgrades

If you’ve got these political parties pulling funding one year and then reinstating it another, or fighting over it because the government shut down, and causing these delays, they can easily turn a short-term project — short-term in the sense of three to five years — into something that takes 10 or 20 or just never happens. [Transportation Secretary Sean ] Duffy says he can’t guarantee this won’t happen again
Does that mean it’s going to happen again? Because it seemed pretty bad on Friday

If I were Sean Duffy, I would definitely be saying that this is probably going to happen again because honestly, it is.  Ironically, we’ve gotten so good at kind of kicking the can down the road and making the best out of these systems for so long that we’re now to the point where all of these Band-Aid fixes are just falling apart all at once
If we had done a little bit more to cause failures five to 10 years ago, then we probably would be in a better place today, in a weird sense
It’s pretty clear that we’ve seen the pace of these aviation infrastructure and equipment crises accelerating over the last three to five years
And it’s really because there’s nothing else that we can do to stop it
You just have to take the pain at some point
And we could have done it earlier with better political will, but now the equipment itself is telling us just can’t go on anymore

Darryl, we famously aren’t the only country with planes, and certainly we can’t be the only country with aging infrastructure.  How are the other countries fixing their aging infrastructure without having to ground all their planes on a Friday night? Europe probably has a very similar system in terms of the age of its components, but they do a lot of domestic travel through trains
The load on the aviation system is substantially less.  US airspace is the most crowded in the entire world, and it’s because we rely on flights to get from point A to point B

Outside of the Northeast, there’s really no alternative if you want to go more than 200 miles and you don’t want to spend a whole day driving.  If you were redoing the system today, like is happening in China, you would just put in this fancy fiber optic stuff
Now obviously, it’s a lot easier when you’ve got a single political system to rip up entire hundred-mile runs of cable without having to go through all of these permitting processes
But what about, dare I ask, Canada? Canada has about 8 to 10 percent of the volume of the United States in terms of air
In fact, Canadian airspace is partially controlled by American air traffic controllers
And Canada actually requires people to pay fees for the infrastructure
In the US, we’ve decided that aviation is essentially a right for people, so the pressure is to push down costs as much as possible

title: The US helped the world rein in nuclear weapons. Could it do the same for AI?
excerpt: The unfinished work of nuclear governance offers an important lesson for those struggling with the risk of AI now: learning to live with a dangerous technology
body: The unfinished work of nuclear governance offers an important lesson for those struggling with the risk of AI now: learning to live with a dangerous technology is not the same as eliminating its threat. | Daniel Gnap/NurPhoto/Getty Images When Illinois Gov

JB Pritzker talks about the threat of artificial intelligence, he offers an increasingly common point of comparison: it is a danger “on the level of nuclear weapons.” The comparison is not far-fetched

If the international community found ways to constrain a potentially catastrophic technology once before, perhaps those arrangements can help us constrain another.  The trouble is that while nuclear nonproliferation may be a useful framework for thinking about regulating AI, it isn’t necessarily a good one
Not because the technologies are too different, but because nuclear nonproliferation hasn’t actually freed us from the prospect of nuclear war

Nevertheless, the unfinished work of nuclear governance offers an important lesson for those struggling with the risk of AI now: learning to live with a dangerous technology is not the same as eliminating its threat.  What we might be able to do, however, is eliminate uncertainty about who’s building AI, what AI is capable of, and when AI puts people at risk
The US has done exactly that with nuclear weapons by declassifying information about the size and condition of its own arsenal, encouraging other nuclear powers to do the same

Prioritizing transparency about AI wouldn’t eliminate the dangers altogether, but it might help us move forward more collectively as we strive to manage the very real risks of this emerging technology

What the nuclear-AI analogy gets right… and wrong Comparisons between AI and nuclear weapons have emerged not just from politicians and commentators but from those at the very top of the frontier AI food chain
For some AI leaders, nuclear weapons also represent an ideal model for oversight

In a 2023 essay , OpenAI’s Sam Altman, Greg Brockman, and Ilya Sutskever called for “something like an [International Atomic Energy Agency] (IAEA) for superintelligence efforts.” Their proposed international authority would “inspect systems, require audits, test for compliance with safety standards,” and restrict how the most powerful systems could be deployed
The goal of such measures is to make the development of superintelligence safe, rather than prevent it, much as nonproliferation regimes stop short of banning nuclear weapons outright

Altman and his colleagues argue that the technology could deliver enormous benefits, while stopping its creation would be “unintuitively risky and difficult.” Not everyone invoking nuclear governance draws the line in the same place

In September, AI researcher Yoshua Bengio told the UN Security Council that “frontier AI should be licensed like… medicine, aviation, and nuclear energy to incentivize safe development.” He also called for a universal constraint on AI development, one more expansive than those imposed on nuclear weapons: “No one, no company and no country, should develop an AI system that could cause large-scale harm.” The real problem with such schemes may be figuring out how they would be enforced — and by whom
Sure, there are fewer states with nuclear weapons today than there could have been if nonproliferation had not become a policy priority for the US
However, this was not the result of diplomatic prowess or good-faith restraint
In the most important cases, it was a result of coercion by the US and its allies

As Christopher David LaRoche and Ankit Panda, two nuclear experts at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, explained in Foreign Affairs: “South Korea and Taiwan gave up nascent weapons programs after intense pressure from the United States…and a threat to pull military support if they did not comply

Israeli airstrikes took out the Iraqi and Syrian programs; Libya surrendered its own under sustained U.S. and British pressure.” In other words, unless the US seeks to go to war to prevent countries around the world from getting hands on frontier AI, nuclear nonproliferation is not the ideal mold for AI regulation
Plus, even in the face of a robust nonproliferation regime, a few states managed to slip through the cracks — India, Israel, North Korea, and Pakistan each acquired nuclear weapons
Despite that, there are still fewer nuclear weapons in the world today than there were at the peak of the Cold War
But even the best-laid plans might not last forever
The arms control agreements that made such disarmament possible have all crumbled — whether due to cheating, repudiation, or expired treaties
Moreover, in addition to the increased number of states in possession of nuclear weapons, China has tripled its number of nuclear weapons just this decade
These are the consequences of a regime built to manage a technology, rather than eliminate it
A similar frontier AI nonproliferation regime would govern who may build the most powerful systems, while leaving unaddressed the question of whether anyone should have that option in the first place
A similar frontier AI nonproliferation regime would govern who may build the most powerful systems, while leaving unaddressed the question of whether anyone should have that option in the first place
The greatest lesson is for the US Today, the threat of nuclear war persists

However, nuclear nonproliferation offers us one powerful takeaway: the United States, in particular, has a tremendous role to play in shaping the future of regulating frontier AI. “In the nuclear domain specifically, the US historically has had a powerful norm-entrepreneurship function,” Panda told me. “What the United States does when it comes to nuclear weapons does get noticed by other countries and often gets adopted by other countries.” This has historically involved leadership in transparency, Panda said. “The US, to its credit, is much more transparent than every other nuclear country when it comes to talking about things like command and control and what we do and don’t do.” For example, the US regularly declassifies and publishes data regarding the size of its nuclear weapons stockpile, fissile material inventories, and production facilities

In a similar way, the US could lead the world in transparency about the frontier AI it is pursuing, the limits it might impose on that technology, and the safeguards in place to keep it under control.  This could take shape in a few ways, beginning with the US government’s own use of AI: Before deploying a powerful and risky AI system, the government could disclose what risks it tested for, the conditions under which the system is considered reliable, its known limitations, and what findings would prevent deployment.  The US could explain which military decisions AI may contribute to and which require human authorization
This might, for example, involve distinguishing intelligence analysis from authority to initiate an attack
The government could also identify military applications of AI that it rules out altogether
The US could publish accounts of failures or unexpected behavior, explaining whether a system was withdrawn, restricted, or retested after something went wrong

These transparency measures should also extend to the private sector, and the government could require companies to: Disclose dangerous-capability testing: This would involve requiring frontier developers to publish standardized summaries of tests for risks such as assisting cyberattacks, contributing to biological weapons development, or operating autonomously beyond intended limits
Report serious incidents and near misses: Developers and deployers could be required to notify a regulator of significant safety failures, breaches, or unexpected dangerous behavior

Publish the conditions for pausing development or withholding release: Companies could disclose in advance which findings would trigger additional safeguards, delay product launches, or halt further development
As AI continues to reshape the world we live in, prioritizing transparency around the technology’s achievements — and limits — is one way to ensure that safety and security remain central

Panda suggested that such measures could reassure adversaries that the US is not going to implement frontier AI models in ways that might be dangerous or irresponsible.

body: In the days after the military operation that ousted Nicolás Maduro , a poll from the Caracas‑based firm Meganálisis showed that 92 percent of Venezuelans were grateful to President Donald Trump for removing Maduro and that 90 percent wanted the US as Venezuela’s main ally
During the months since, the US has been heavily involved in shaping Venezuela’s future

But some key reforms are moving slower than Venezuelans hoped for.  US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has laid out a three-step plan for US intervention in Venezuela : stability, recovery, and a transition to democracy
While plans for political reforms and democratic elections in Venezuela are moving slowly, the designs for who controls its oil have been moving fast

The US recently announced an agreement with Venezuela as “ the biggest oil deal in world history .” As Venezuelans hold out hope that the final step in Rubio’s plan, a transition to democracy, will still materialize, support among Venezuelans for Trump appears to be slipping
According to a new Meganálisis poll, 83 percent of Venezuelans don’t believe Trump wants what is best for their countr y

As voices grow louder from opposition leaders like Nobel Peace Prize winner María Corina Machado to jumpstart democratic processes, pressure on the US is mounting to make good on their promise.  Hosted by Kahlil Greene , this video is part of our new series, Kahlil Explains , that unites Vox’s unique brand of explainer journalism with Greene’s expertise in how politics and culture shape society

title: A perfect storm is descending on the AI industry
excerpt: An aerial view of a 33 megawatt data center with closed-loop cooling system on April 14, 2026 in Vernon, California. | Mario Tama/Getty Images The stock market
body: An aerial view of a 33 megawatt data center with closed-loop cooling system on April 14, 2026 in Vernon, California. | Mario Tama/Getty Images The stock market is set to christen a new trillion-dollar company on Wednesday, as the AI juggernaut Anthropic goes public
Key takeaways Fears of an AI market crash are growing, with tech stocks sliding sharply since June
The AI industry is spending far more on infrastructure than it earns, and cheaper “good enough” models threaten the profits of frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic
Three recent shocks have made things worse
The boom may survive, but AI companies can no longer count on governments deferring to them or markets cheering them on

The IPO should have been the crowning triumph of the AI boom — a testament to the technology’s mind-bending commercial value, which enabled a seven-person startup to become a world-conquering juggernaut in five short years

Even as investors scramble to claim a piece of our future God-emperor, Claude Opus 5,000 ( hallowed be his name! ), fears of an AI market crash are building.  Since June, tech stocks have taken a beating, with one generative AI ETF shedding 35 percent of its value
Over the same period, the Philadelphia semiconductor index — a rough gauge of the chip industry’s value — fell by more than one-third

The sell-off gained steam in recent weeks, as Republicans lost key elections to AI-skeptical Democrats — and Nvidia lost its longtime CEO to a geopolitically explosive sex scandal, a leadership change that has overshadowed the company’s persistently strong earnings

Meanwhile, every mysterious IT problem at a major government institution or company is being scrutinized for signs of AI hacking — which could bring even more unwanted attention from politicians, regulators, and the general public.  Now, after years of deriding the AI boom as a “bubble,” some of the industry’s bears are finally hearing a popping sound: In their estimation, the bubble has already burst .  Such declarations are premature
To qualify as a punctured bubble, the decline in AI assets would need to become much deeper and more sustained than it’s been thus far

As of this writing, the tech-heavy Nasdaq index remains more than 4 percent higher than it was when the year began.  Nevertheless, there is an increasingly strong case for believing that investors drastically overvalued AI-related companies, and that recent events might speed the AI industry toward a day of financial reckoning
At the very least, the AI boom’s charmed childhood seems to be giving way to a more troubled adolescence

And given the centrality of artificial intelligence to today’s economy, a large-enough correction could tip the US into a recession , thereby raising unemployment, squeezing wages, and quite possibly accelerating the automation of white-collar jobs — all of which could exacerbate Big Tech’s political headaches.     “Once the fever breaks, it never really comes back,” Brent Donnelly, a former HSBC trader and president of the financial media company Spectra Markets, told me. “People aren’t going to be as optimistic now that the cracks have begun to show.” AI bubble-o-nomics 101 Financial analysts have been wringing their hands over a potential AI bubble for years
And not without reason.  The AI boom’s scale alone makes a case for its unsustainability
According to Goldman Sachs, US investment in AI infrastructure this year will reach $581 billion, or roughly 1.8 percent of America’s entire GDP

Next year, the bank expects such capital expenditures will add up to 2.5 percent of our nation’s total economy.  For context, at the peak of the dot-com boom in 2000, spending on telecommunications and fiber totaled only 1.15 percent of America’s gross domestic product
In terms of magnitude, the closer analog to today’s AI frenzy might be the railroad buildout of the late 19th century
View Link Of course, both the dot-com and railroad booms ended in tears
Investors weren’t wrong to think that trains and the internet would prove immensely valuable
But in their excitement about each technology’s promise, they overestimated near-term demand for many rail lines and fiber optic cables
And there’s reason to think that today’s AI investors are making a similar mistake
According to an estimate from the consulting firm Bain & Company, the AI industry will need to generate $6 trillion in annual revenues by 2031 to justify its spending on data centers and chips

The sector’s current revenues are closer to $540 billion, according to an estimate from Grandview Research .  Thus, tech investors are essentially betting that demand for AI is poised to soar at a mind-bending rate.  Yet this hope may rest on a faulty extrapolation from Silicon Valley’s own experience
Artificial intelligence has rapidly penetrated the software industry, delivering large productivity gains in the process
But outside of tech, corporate interest has been more tepid
According to a 2026 NBER study, just 2 percent of firms account for over half of AI enterprise spending

And among companies that deployed AI, 80 percent discerned no productivity benefits from the technology. “There’s a lot of real revenue being generated by these companies,” Paulo Carvão, an ex-IBM executive and research fellow at Harvard’s Kennedy School, said. “But the amount of investments and infrastructure far outweigh revenue-generating capabilities and there is no clear path towards these lines crossing.” Finally, even if AI sales skyrocket, the major labs could still prove radically less profitable than markets are wagering

To justify their trillion-dollar valuations, OpenAI and Anthropic don’t merely need other companies to spend vastly more on artificial intelligence; they also need them to pay a premium for frontier models, even as cheaper knock-offs become more and more adept. (Disclosure: Vox Media is one of several publishers that have signed partnership agreements with OpenAI
Our reporting remains editorially independent.) Yet for most corporations, that might be a losing proposition
Today, the second-tier AI systems aren’t just a little cheaper than the frontier ones
The Chinese open-weight model Kimi K3.1 Pro costs $10 per million tokens of output ; for OpenAI’s most advanced model, GPT-6 Astra, that figure is $50
Perhaps, this premium is justified, given the current divergence between each product’s abilities
But that gap might become less relevant as AI becomes more powerful.  After all, intelligence has diminishing returns in many fields of endeavor
To staff its accounting department, Taco Bell could hire a team of path-breaking theoretical mathematicians

But if those geniuses cost five times as much as your average CPA, it would probably be wiser for the company to go with the latter; you simply don’t need a Fields medalist to monitor gordita revenues

Likewise, once last year’s AI model is as capable as 10,000 geniuses, few companies may feel the need to pay extra for a bot that’s as skilled as 10,500.  Already, there is some evidence that businesses consider open-source models good enough for many purposes

In a September survey of 200 enterprises, the market analysis firm Futurum Research found that 53 percent had partially substituted open-weight models for frontier ones.  “For the financial modeling that I do — which isn’t rocket science but not fourth-grade math either — Claude is already so capable, I can’t really imagine what more the next 6.0 or 7.0 would offer me,” Spectra’s Donnelly told me. “There was an all-you-can-eat buffet approach initially where token budgets weren’t really a huge consideration
But now that it’s not free, people are looking for cheaper options.” The autumn of the AI industry’s discontent These basic concerns have long shadowed the AI boom

Every time investors started getting antsy, however, a new technical breakthrough or eye-popping earnings report seemed to quell their fears.  But concerns about a bubble intensified in recent weeks, for at least three reasons: 1) The “central bank” of the AI sector is in crisis

title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
excerpt: Record-low hydropower in the Southwest: The US Southwest generated 28% less hydropower than its 10-year average this past spring and summer, driven by a 27-year
body: Record-low hydropower in the Southwest: The US Southwest generated 28% less hydropower than its 10-year average this past spring and summer, driven by a 27-year drought
That has pushed the region's two largest reservoirs, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, dangerously close to the minimum levels needed to generate electricity

Climate change is making things worse: Rising temperatures mean less snow to fill reservoirs, more droughts, and increasingly unpredictable precipitation, a combination that can make hydropower less reliable
The emissions ripple effect: When hydropower falters, the consequences extend beyond the power grid

A global shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for roughly 40% of the 1.1% rise in energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions in 2023, according to the International Energy Agency. " data-chronoton-post-id="1148742" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration
Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs
The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand
But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases
Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River

And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows.  Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants
At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant
The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September

Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people.  Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years

Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world.  The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less.  But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study

Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable.  Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA
El Niño could provide some temporary relief
Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US
Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low
But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions
Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher
In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally
A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.
